1. Introduction

Randwick City's heritage is rich and diverse and includes buildings, structures, Aboriginal and archaeological sites, parks and reserves. They are valued because they are associated with significant phases of history, or with important people and events in Randwick's development and cultural heritage. Collectively, this heritage contributes to the community's cultural life, sense of place, and shared identity, fostering pride and continuity across generations.

It is important to recognise that the legal owners of a state or local heritage-listed property are not merely owners, but custodians entrusted with the care of a significant cultural asset. While they have a legal responsibility, they also have a unique opportunity to help preserve and celebrate the significance and character of these places for future generations. By maintaining and respecting heritage features, owners contribute to a shared sense of identity and help keep the stories of our community alive.

Heritage is a living part of our environment, and its preservation is a collaborative effort that benefits everyone.

This section of the DCP applies to heritage listed items and heritage conservation areas (HCAs) identified under Schedule 5 of the Randwick Local Environmental Plan 2012 (RLEP) and should be read in conjunction with other sections of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the application.

Where there are inconsistencies between this section and any other DCP sections, this section will prevail.

General objectives

The general objectives of this section of the DCP are to:

  • Retain and conserve Randwick's rich and diverse environmental heritage .
  • Provide detailed guidelines to manage change to the environmental heritage of Randwick as defined and identified in RLEP
  • Ensure development proposals consider the impacts to the cultural significance of heritage items, HCAs, archaeological sites, and places of Aboriginal cultural significance.

1.1. Burra Charter

The Australia ICOMOS Charter for the Conservation of Places of Cultural Significance (the Burra Charter) is widely adopted as the standard guidelines for heritage conservation in Australia and sets out a standard of practice for those who provide advice, make decisions about or undertaking works to places of cultural significance, including owners, managers and custodians.

Development affecting a heritage item or property within an HCA is assessed having regard to the principles and practices contained in the Burra Charter .

F or the purposes of this DCP, 'Cultural Significance' (significance), 'Fabric' , 'maintenance', 'preservation', 'restoration', 'reconstruction', 'adaptation', 'use', 'compatible' and 'setting' definitions are based on the Australia ICOMOS Charter for the Conservation of Places of Cultural Significance 2013 (Burra Charter).

Cultural significance means aesthetic, historic, scientific, social or spiritual value for past, present or future generations. Cultural significance is embodied in the place itself, its fabric, setting, use, associations, meanings, records, related places and related objects. Places may have a range of values for different individuals or groups.

Fabric means all the physical material of the place including elements, fixtures, contents and objects. Fabric includes building interiors and sub-surface remains, as well as excavated material. Natural elements i.e. bed rocks of a place may also constitute fabric. Fabric may define spaces and views, and these may be part of the significance of the place.

Maintenance means the continuous protective care of a place, and its setting. Maintenance is to be distinguished from repair which involves restoration or reconstruction.

Preservation means maintaining a place in its existing state and retarding deterioration.

Restoration means returning a place to a known earlier state by removing accretions or by reassembling existing elements without the introduction of new material.

Reconstruction means returning a place to a known earlier state and is distinguished from restoration by the introduction of new material. New material may include recycled material salvaged from other places. This should not be to the detriment of any place of cultural significance.

Adaptation means changing a place to suit the existing use or a proposed use.

Use means the functions of a place, including the activities and traditional and customary practices that may occur at the place or are dependent on the place.

Compatible Use means a use which respects the cultural significance of a place. Such a use involves no, or minimal, impact on cultural significance.

Setting means the immediate and extended environment of a place that is part of or contributes to its cultural significance and distinctive character. Setting may include structures, spaces, land, water, and sky; the visual setting including views to and from the place, and along a cultural route; and other sensory aspects of the setting such as smells and sounds. Setting may also include historical and contemporary relationships, such as use and activities, social and spiritual practices, and relationships with other places, both tangible and intangible.

1.2. Heritage places in Randwick City

This DCP section applies to the environmental heritage within Randwick City as identified in the RLEP:

  • Heritage items (local, state, and national)

Heritage conservation areas

  • Archaeological sites
  • Aboriginal heritage (places and objects)

The requirements, objectives and controls in this section apply in addition to the heritage conservation requirements, principles and practices contained in the Burra Charter, RLEP Clause 5.10 , policy guidelines contained in the Heritage Inventory Assessment Report (State Heritage Inventory Report available online at the Department of Environment's heritage website), development requirements of other relevant parts of this DCP, and relevant conservation management plans.

Heritage items, HCAs some archaeological sites and Aboriginal places and significant landscape elements and geological sites are listed in Schedule 5 of the RLEP.

1.3. Heritage advice

Prior to lodging a Development Application (DA) or undertaking maintenance works to a heritage item or a property located within an HCA, or if works are likely to affect an Aboriginal object, Aboriginal place of cultural significance or historical archaeological site, applicants are advised to discuss their proposal with Council's specialist Heritage Officer.

Where major work is proposed, applicants are strongly advised to obtain professional assistance from a recognised expert in heritage conservation.

1.4. Consent requirements

1.4.1. Development not requiring consent

Heritage Exemption Certificate for maintenance and repair works to Local items listed under the Randwick Local Environmental Plan

Maintenance and repair works are encouraged for heritage items and properties in HCAs and may not require development consent from Council if they are of a minor nature and would not adversely affect the significance of the item or HCA.

Applicants must consult with Council prior to undertaking any maintenance or repair works to confirm whether development consent (i.e. a Development Application) is required. A written advice must be obtained from Council prior to the commencement of any works.

Where it is determined that the proposed works do not require development consent, and relate to a heritage item or property within a Heritage Conservation Area, the applicant must obtain a Heritage Exemption Certificate (HEC) from Council prior to commencing works.

A Heritage Exemption Certificate application form can be found on Council's website or HERITAGE-MINOR-WORKS-WITHOUT-CONSENT.pdf.

Maintenance and repairs can include non-structural external works such as:

  • Essential maintenance and reinstatement of original heritage features
  • Replacing broken windows frames, panes and fly screens
  • Minor repairs to roofing, brickwork, timberwork, metal work, fencing and tessellated tiles
  • Repainting surfaces which are already painted, including timberwork and metalwork
  • Repointing brickwork and masonry

Maintenance and repairs can also include non-structural internal works such as:

  • Patching, painting and decoration to the interior of the building
  • Installation of joinery
  • Repairing timber floors
  • Plumbing and gas fitting work
  • Electrical work and communications cabling
  • Installation of insulation

Additionally, the installation of solar panels and associated equipment within a HCA may be considered under a HEC, if they provided the works do not involve:

  • Solar panels positioned on the primary roofs or verandahs facing/visible from the main street
  • Heritage items that form part of a continuous group or row of properties
  • Slate or timber shingle roofs
  • Complex primary street facing roofs
  • Very small primary street facing roofs (smaller than 4m)
  • Any works that require structural modifications to support the solar panels
  • Any works that involving removal of roof elements, such as chimneys, capping, parapet walls.

Further, the installation of surveillance systems and devices on heritage items and within HCAs may be considered where they:

  • are not visible from the public domain
  • do not involve alteration, damage or the removal of significant fabric.

Any new penetrations must be limited in number and made through non-significant fabric or mortar joints only.

Exempt development

Under the State Environmental Planning Policy Exempt and Complying Development Codes 2008 (The Codes SEPP) some categories of minor internal works are permitted as Exempt Development for buildings within HCAs, but not for heritage items. The classification of Exempt Development refers to works that have minimal environmental impact and therefore does not require Council's consent. The Codes SEPP does not permit external building alterations to heritage items or properties located within HCAs.

Standard exemption for State Heritage Register items

Certain activities and work are exempt from approval under the Heritage Act 1977 for items listed on the State Heritage Register or subject to an interim heritage order. Standard exemptions include maintenance works where t hese have little to no impact on the item's heritage significance and support its ongoing management.

These standard exemptions are made under the Heritage Act 1977 and published in the NSW Government Gazette - https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/heritage/apply-for-heritageapprovals-and-permits/state-heritage-register-items/standard-exemptions

Before any activity or work takes place, follow these steps to:

  • understand what 'significant fabric' is
  • determine if your proposed activity or work can be carried out under a standard exemption and therefore you do not need to lodge an application for approval
  • understand how to comply with standard exemption requirements.

Note

To determine if a property is heritage listed, search the State Heritage Inventory online database using the Heritage NSW website, or check Schedule 5 of RLEP and Heritage Map. You can also search the Australian Heritage Database for National listings and inquire with Council or Heritage NSW for the most accurate information.

1.4.2. Development requiring consent

A DA is required for the carrying out of development which relates to a heritage item, development in an HCA, Aboriginal place or archaeological site. RLEP Clause 5.10 (2) identifies those instances where development consent is required.

Additionally, it is important to carefully consider the following guidelines for DAs impacting Aboriginal objects and places of cultural significance, historical archaeological sites, and state listed heritage items.

Aboriginal objects and places of cultural heritage

Aboriginal objects and places provide evidence relating to Aboriginal habitation of an area and are of cultural significance to Aboriginal people because of their spiritual, ceremonial, historic, social or educational values. Aboriginal objects and places are protected under the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974.

Part 4 of Schedule 5 under the RLEP identifies the former Prince Henry Hospital site as an area containing Aboriginal cultural heritage. Other Aboriginal objects and places in Randwick City are not listed in the RLEP due to the sensitive nature of these sites. This is common practice for protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage in NSW.

Development consent is required to disturb or excavate land containing Aboriginal objects or an Aboriginal place. It is an offence to harm or desecrate an Aboriginal object or place. If Aboriginal objects are present or likely to be present and an activity will harm those objects, an Aboriginal Heritage Impact Permit (AHIP) will be required.

Clause 5.10(8) -Aboriginal Places of Heritage Significance - , Council may require a Statement of Heritage Impact to assist in its consideration of the effect of the proposed development on the cultural significance of the Aboriginal object or place, or to identify the potential for the discovery of Aboriginal cultural heritage on a particular site. As part of the heritage impact assessment, consultation with local Aboriginal groups must be undertaken and the outcomes of such consultation provided to Council with a development application.

Historical Archaeological sites

Archaeological sites provide physical evidence of the past and can include objects and artefacts from the lives of previous generations, such as tools and household items, as well as remains of early buildings and structures.

A number of archaeological sites are listed in Schedule 5 of the RLEP. Archaeological sites or relics that have local or state significance are protected under the NSW Heritage Act 1977.

Development consent is required for disturbing or excavating an archaeological site while knowing or suspecting that the work may result in a relic being discovered, exposed, moved, damaged or destroyed. Council may request an archaeological assessment to confirm the likelihood and potential significance of relics on the site and recommend appropriate action in the context of the proposed development.

When intending to disturb or excavate land where such archaeological relics have been identified or are considered likely to occur, it is the responsibility of the property owner to seek relevant approvals, including an excavation permit or an exception under Section 139 and Section 140 of the Heritage Act 1977.

RLEP Clause 5.10(7) Archaeological Sites outlines consultation requirements with respect to carrying out development on an archaeological site.

State Heritage Register items

Heritage items of State significance are listed on the NSW State Heritage Register (SHR) and should be identified under Schedule 5 of the RLEP. The NSW Heritage Council is the consent authority for any development proposal affecting SHR Items under the NSW Heritage Act 1977.

Consent from the NSW Heritage Council requires either the submission of an Integrated DA, or a prior Section 60 application under the NSW Heritage Act 1977. Applicants are advised to consult with either Council or the Heritage NSW, in relation to works affecting SHR Items.

Note

To view the Codes SEPP, refer to www.legislation.nsw.gov.au Further information on permits relating to Aboriginal objects and places of significance, obtaining approvals relating to archaeological sites, and NSW Heritage Register is available from the NSW Department of Environment and Heritage: www.environment.nsw.gov.au

1.4.3. Development in the vicinity of heritage items and heritage conservation areas

All development adjacent to or in the vicinity of a heritage item or HCA must carefully consider its potential impact on cultural significance, fabric, and setting of the item and/or HCA. Applicants should address any potential impacts of the development on a heritage item or HCA and measures to mitigate this impact in their Statement of Environmental Effects and/or Statement of Heritage Impact (SOHI).

The proposal must also consider how development may impact on heritage items and HCAs in neighbouring's LGAs (i.e. Daceyville in Bayside LGA).

1.4.4. Infill buildings

A new building within a heritage conservation area, referred to as an infill building, must be designed to respect and be sensitive to its heritage context. It should be sympathetic to neighbouring buildings in terms of established setbacks, scale, form and materials.

New development must reflect the established site coverage pattern and urban grain of the original subdivision and development of the suburb. In accordance with the Burra Charter principles, infill buildings should be clearly identifiable as contemporary additions and must not attempt to replicate historic buildings or mimic traditional detailing.

Note

For further guidance refer to 'Design in Context: Guidelines for Infill Development in the Historic Environment' jointly produced by the Heritage Council of NSW and the Royal Australian Institute of Architects (NSW Chapter).

1.4.5. Adaptive reuse

Council supports the continuation of the original use of a heritage building as it helps retain the original floorplan, decorative features and enhances cultural significance. However, where continuation is not feasible due to changes in technology and market/social trends, adaptive reuse of a heritage item may be considered acceptable on heritage grounds.

Development must comply with the Burra Charter definition and guideline for 'compatible use':

Compatible use respects the cultural significance of the place and involves no or minimal impact on cultural significance.

Where the original use of a place is of cultural significance it should be retained wherever possible (e.g. Post Office, Bank, Religious, Educational, Library, etc.).

Note

Refer to 'New Uses for Heritage Places: Guidelines for the Adaptation of Historic Buildings and Sites' prepared by the Heritage Branch, Office of Heritage and Environment, for further guidance on the adaptation of heritage buildings.

1.5. Heritage management documents

Heritage conservation management plans

A Conservation Management Plan/Schedule (CMP/S) and/or a Heritage Asset Action Plan (HAAP) may be required where Council considers that the significance of a heritage item or a contributory item and the extent of proposed changes warrant a more detailed and rigorous assessment.

A CMP/S or HAAP identify conservation polices and management mechanisms to ensure the cultural significance of a place is retained. They are particularly useful where building fabric has deteriorated, and to facilitate master planning of larger sites and long-term asset management is needed. A CMP/S or HAAP must be prepared by a specialist heritage consultant. RLEP Clause 5.10(6) of the Randwick LEP outlines HCMP/S or HAAP considerations relevant to the CMP/S and HAAP preparation.

Statement of Heritage Impact

A Statement of Heritage Impact (SOHI) - also referred to as a heritage impact assessment - evaluates the extent to which a proposal may affect the significance of a heritage item or HCA. A SOHI must establish the cultural significance of a place, assess the impact of the proposed development on that significance, and propose design and planning measures to mitigate adverse impacts.

A SOHI is generally required for development effecting heritage significance of a heritage item or a HCA, archaeological sites, and Aboriginal places and objects. A SOHI may also be required for development adjacent to or in the vicinity of a heritage item or HCA, where there is potential for indirect heritage impact.

For major changes or alterations, the required SOHI must be prepared by a specialist heritage consultant who can advise on alternative design solutions to reduce heritage impacts.

Note

For more guidance, refer to 'Assessing Heritage Significance' and 'Statements of Heritage Impact' (2023) prepared by the then Department of Planning and Environment (DPE). Council's Heritage Planner can also clarify whether a DA requires the submission of a Heritage Impact Statement, Heritage Conservation Management Plan, and Heritage Asset Action Plan. Additional resources on preparing a Heritage Conservation Management Plan and Heritage Asset Action Plan are available at Heritage NSW

2. Development controls

2.1. Heritage items and Heritage Conservation Areas

Explanation

This section contains objectives and controls to protect and enhance Randwick City's heritage items and HCAs. It aims to ensure that development affecting heritage items or properties within HCAs or within the vicinity of an item or a HCA is sympathetic to the heritage values by achieving a balanced approach between contemporary design expectations, environmental sustainability, embodied energy, character, and protecting cultural significance.

Buildings and sites within HCAs are identified on the DCP map as being contributory, neutral, or detracting to the character and significance of the HCA.

Contributory buildings provide good evidence of the main development period(s) and make a positive contribution to the character and/or heritage significance of HCAs. They have a collective significance, and their retention is essential if the character of the area is to be maintained.

Non-contributory (neutral and detracting) buildings may have limited historic values but nonetheless respects the surrounding context or display qualities which do not add to the character of the heritage conservation area. They are not to be considered as a precedent for new work when assessing the merit of an application. Non-contributory buildings may be demolished and replaced by new development sympathetic to the character of the heritage conservation area.

Objectives

  • P rotect and enhance Randwick City's heritage items and HCAs
  • Ensure development and alterations and additions to heritage items and/or within an HCA respects and does not distort, obscure or detract from the cultural significance of the place or its interpretation and appreciation
  • Ensure the adaptive reuse of heritage items enhances its historic and cultural significance and does not result the unnecessary removal of significant fabric.

Controls

All development

  • All new development in an HCA or in the vicinity of a HCA or a heritage item must respect the design, scale and character of neighbouring buildings and the key heritage values of the item and the area
  • All development proposals within, adjacent to, or in the vicinity of a heritage item or HCA must demonstrate that they have considered the likely impact on cultural significance and fabric of the item and/or HCA
  • Proposals to alter or add to a heritage item or a building in an HCA must consider assessment of the significance of individual building elements, the broader area, and the relationship to neighbouring properties and the streetscape
  • Alterations and additions to heritage items and contributory buildings must be designed and sited to retain contributory features of the building and maintain the streetscape character of the HCA
  • A new building, or additions visible from the street or an HCA, must respect and respond to the HCA and streetscape character. A detailed streetscape analysis must be included in the site analysis submitted with any DA
  • When proposing adaptive reuse of a heritage item, the proposal must ensure that the significance and original fabric of the heritage item is not adversely affected by the change of use
  • Alterations and additions to group items must consider the impacts on the entire group, in particular the existing pattern of rear additions and location of alterations.

Neutral buildings

  • Alterations and additions to a neutral building must:
  • remove unsympathetic alterations and additions, including inappropriate building elements
  • ii) respect the original building 's bulk, form, scale and height
  • iii) minimise removal of heritage fabric and building elements
  • iv) use appropriate and sympathetic materials, finishes and colours that complement the HCA and do not diminish its significance.
  • Demolition of neutral buildings will only be considered where it can be demonstrated:
  • restoration of the building is not reasonable
  • ii) the replacement building will enhance and not compromise the significance of the HCA.
  • Where demolition of a neutral building is approved, Council may require a photographic archival record of the building to be submitted to Council as a condition of consent.

Detracting buildings

  • Development on sites containing detracting buildings must aim to improve the contribution of the site to the character of the HCA
  • Alterations and additions to, or redevelopment of, detracting buildings must:
  • remove inappropriate and unsympathetic additions and modifications that are intrusive to the significance of the HCA
  • ii) respect the prevailing bulk, form, scale and height of the surrounding streetscape.
  • Contemporary design is acceptable where it is sympathetic to the character of the HCA and/or nearby heritage items.

2.2. Demolition and excavation

Demolition of a heritage item or contributory building in a heritage conservation area is generally not supported, unless there are overriding reasons such as structural damage. The demolition of a non-contributory building and replacement by an appropriately designed infill building can be supported where carefully demonstrated (refer to section 2.1 above).

In assessing a DA for the demolition of a heritage item or a contributory building, Council will consider:

  • The heritage significance of the item or building
  • The structural condition
  • Comparative analysis of all options; and
  • The contribution the item or building makes to the streetscape.

Council may require the submission of a report by a structural engineer with heritage experience to determine whether the building is, or is not, structurally capable of reasonable and economic use.

Where demolition of a heritage item or a contributory building within a heritage conservation area is approved it will generally be conditional upon the submission of a photographic archival recording using either film or digital capture to provide a stable and long-term record. A photographic plan sheet of the building should be used to show the location and direction of all photographs and the sequence in which they were taken. The Heritage Branch guidelines include requirements for cameras, film and digital image storage. Applications for demolition of a heritage item or buildings in a heritage conservation area are required to provide details on the replacement development.

Excavation beneath, adjacent to, or in front of early buildings has the potential to compromise their structural integrity is generally not supported. To assess the impact of excavation applicants must provide detailed information on:

  • The nature and method of construction
  • The structural condition of all buildings on the site
  • The potential impacts on neighbouring heritage-listed buildings and HCA properties
  • The ground conditions of the site and adjoining properties

General controls

  • Demolition of heritage items and contributory buildings is not permitted
  • Excavation will not be permitted where:
  • o it occurs under a heritage item or common walls and footings, freestanding boundary walls, or under any other part of a heritage item
  • o it occurs beneath or forward of the front façade of a heritage item
  • Where excavation is proposed beneath and/or within 1.5m of a heritage item, adjacent heritage items or buildings within an HCA, a Geotechnical Report and Structural Report must be prepared by a professional with heritage experience to demonstrate that the works will not have any adverse effect on the structural integrity of those items.

2.3. Design and character

Explanation

The design of new development should achieve a sympathetic blend of old and new, maintaining the heritage character of the area while allowing for contemporary expression. This can be achieved by respecting the established scale, form, siting, setbacks, materials and finishes of the streetscape without being overly imitative. Careful attention must be paid to adjacent development within the vicinity of heritage items and the character of HCA.

Objectives

  • Promote high quality design that complements and enhances the streetscape character and significance of the heritage item or HCA
  • Ensure new development does not adversely impact on the setting, streetscape character or views associated with any heritage item or HCA
  • Ensure additions or changes to the external appearance of heritage items and contributory buildings within HCAs respect the original, built form, architectural style and character

Controls

All development

  • Development must demonstrate how it respects or responds to the heritage values of the heritage item or the HCA (including within the statements of significance of the item or the HCA and its key characteristics outlined in Section 4 of this DCP)
  • A streetscape analysis must be prepared to demonstrate how the development has identified, incorporated, and enhanced the contributory character elements and features of the streetscape such as view corridors, built form, scale, setbacks, fencing styles, extent of soft landscaping, significant trees/landscape elements and garages and driveway locations. A streetscape analysis must be prepared and submitted to Council for review at DA stage
  • New development should be consistent with important horizontal elements of buildings in the streetscape, in particular ground floor levels and eaves lines, where appropriate
  • Large blank areas of brick or rendered walls should be avoided. Where this is not possible, contrasting building materials and treatments must be used to break up the visual mass
  • Alterations, extensions, or additions to the building, and its grounds, that are considered visually or architecturally incompatible with the original character of the site must be removed. Unsympathetic elements should be replaced with new works that are designed to be in harmony with the original building style, scale, materials, and detailing. Original features should be reinstated using materials, construction techniques, and forms that closely match or replicate the original design, ensuring the heritage significance and visual integrity of the property are preserved or enhanced.

Heritage items and contributory buildings

  • Street-facing elevations and visible side elevations must not be significantly altered. Additions must be located to the rear or side of the building to minimise visual impact on the streetscape
  • Additions or alterations must complement the existing building in scale, form and detailing while remaining visibly distinguishable from the original fabric on close inspection. New and old design are not to be confused, or the boundaries/junctions blurred.
  • New work must respect and retain the significant heritage fabric, including internal and external features and proportions, chimneys, fireplaces, doors, windows, openings, balconies, and verandas.

2.4. Scale and form

Explanation

Bulk and scale refer to the height and size of a building, while form and massing relate to the arrangement of its component parts. In heritage contexts, these elements must be carefully managed to ensure new development does not dominate or detract from existing heritage significance.

Objectives

  • Ensure that alterations and additions to heritage items and contributory buildings and other development, including buildings, structures, and works within and in the vicinity of HCAs are consistent with the scale and form of these items or contributory buildings, and do not dominate or compete with the heritage significance, including fabric, design, form, scale, character, and setting
  • Ensure that scale and form of new development is consistent with the heritage significance and character of the HCA, and adjacent heritage items and/or contributory buildings

Controls

All development

  • In streetscapes characterised by consistent single storey development, upper-floor additions are only appropriate if not readily visible from the street/public domain. Ground floor rear additions are the preferred form of development
  • Attic style additions may be permissible, where they are sympathetic to the original roof form and not visible from the street/public domain especially for previously unaltered buildings or semi-detached pairs
  • Front dormer windows are discouraged on heritage and contributory items and on relatively unaltered semi-detached pair or terrace rows as they detract from the integrity of the original roof forms and consistency of the streetscape
  • Dormer windows and skylights must not be located on street elevations or where they would be visually prominent from a public domain or detract from the original roof form. Dormer windows must be sympathetic in scale and form, proportion, and detailing to the architectural style of the building.

Heritage items and contributory buildings

  • Additions to existing buildings, and other development on the same site, must be subordinate to the original building, and must not visually dominate, compete with, or obscure its form and massing, including significant roof forms
  • Additions to heritage items, and other associated development, must not introduce prominent design elements that compete with or detract from the architectural features, materials, or detailing of the existing building
  • Single storey rear additions to dwelling houses must be designed so as not to compromise the form and integrity of the main roof, and must be lower in scale and visually subordinate to it
  • Development proposal to the main roof of single storey dwelling houses may be acceptable where they are wholly contained within the existing roof space and do not alter the roof form, pitch, or eaves height
  • Additions to single storey dwelling houses, particularly two storey additions, should adopt a pavilion-style form, comprising a secondary addition connected to the original building by a lower-scale link, to maintain the visual primacy of the original building. Additions to any single storey dwelling house should preferably use pavilion-type forms, with a lower scale link between the original building and any new two storey addition
  • Where a pavilion-style form is not feasible or appropriate, an upper floor addition may be acceptable if it is:
  • located significantly to the rear of the building
  • designed to minimise visual impact on the principal roof form
  • discreet or not visible when viewed from the public domain
  • Unless site-specific controls provide otherwise, within a Heritage Conservation Area, an upper-level addition must not be visible above the ridge line or parapet of the existing building when viewed from the opposite side of the primary street
  • Where rear lanes exist, additional floor space should be provided in a rear outbuilding, rather than an upper-level addition to the principal dwelling
  • Rear additions to semi-detached dwellings must not compromise the symmetry or integrity of the front elevation, and must not visually dominate the adjoining dwelling in the pair, including but not limited to its form, massing original roof form
  • Rear additions to attached dwellings (e.g. terrace houses) must not compromise the integrity of the front elevation or the form of intact rear wings, including but not limited to original roof forms
  • Development must not compromise the integrity of an intact or original roof form of heritage or contributory items.

Non-contributory buildings

  • The scale and form of new buildings must be compatible with the streetscape character, typically single storey, or single storey at the front with two storeys to the rear. The roof form and articulation must also be sympathetic and enhance the heritage and streetscape character.
