1. Introduction

Randwick City has a rich diversity of natural, cultural and scenic landscapes including significant areas of remnant bushland, wetlands and habitat corridors. These natural assets contribute to the City's unique character and ecological significance.

Landscaping plays an essential role in integrating development into the surrounding streetscape and neighbourhood. It enhances the visual amenity and usability of sites, supports recreation and leisure, preserves natural areas and contributes to improved stormwater management, environmental performance and micro-climatic conditions. Implementing the green grid, protecting areas of bushland and biodiversity, increasing tree canopy and increasing the native and indigenous species across the LGA are key priorities of the City of Randwick environment strategy 2022 and our Local strategic Planning statement 2023.

A healthy urban forest provides significant aesthetic, ecological and environmental benefits to residents, workers and visitors to Randwick City.

The long term protection and enhancement of Randwick's urban environment - through the preservation and management of trees and vegetation is essential to achieving the goals set out in the Randwick Environment Strategy, including:

  • Increasing native and indigenous plantings
  • Expanding urban canopy cover
  • Improving connectivity between bushland areas and habitat corridors

This Part of the DCP outlines controls for preparing landscape plans and addressing landscape design matters, including controls for development in and near areas of biodiversity significance and habitat corridors. It aligns with State Environmental Planning Policy Biodiversity and Conservation 2021 (BC SEPP), which includes provisions for the protection and preservation of trees and vegetation.

Vegetation clearing associated with development requiring consent will be assessed as part of the development assessment process and may also require additional assessment under the NSW Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016.

This Part of the DCP applies to all development that impacts existing habitat or includes landscaping and governs the clearing of vegetation that falls below the Biodiversity Offset Scheme threshold outlined in the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016.

For the purposes of Part 2.3 of the BC SEPP, the following vegetation is declared to be vegetation to which the BC SEPP applies:

  • Any vegetation on l and identified as 'Biodiversity' on the Terrestrial Biodiversity Map in RLEP
  • Any vegetation on land zoned Environmental Conservations C2 in the RLEP
  • Any vegetation on Land identified as ' Biodiversity Habitat Corridor' in SSROC Connected Corridors for Biodiversity map.

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

  • Part A - Introduction and other sections
  • Part B5 - Preservation of Trees

Alignment with other planning instruments

In addition to the RLEP, the BC SEPP applies.

In the event of an inconsistency between this DCP and the SEPP, the SEPP prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.

Note

The Sydney Green Grid is a strategic planning framework developed by the NSW Government Architect to create a connected network of green open spaces - parks, bushland, waterways, and tree-lined streets - across Greater Sydney.

Its goal is to ensure that every resident lives within walking distance of quality green space while improving urban resilience, ecological health, and liveability.

The Green Grid is given effect to the NSW planning system through the Greater Sydney Region Plan - A Metropolis of Three Cities (2018) and the Eastern City District Plan 2018.

2. General provisions

Landscaping forms an integral part of site planning and contributes significantly to the visual quality, environmental performance, and overall amenity of development. The integration of natural and designed landscape elements supports ecological resilience, reinforces local character, and provides functional, aesthetic and microclimatic benefits to occupants and the surrounding community.

These provisions establish consistent requirements for the design, implementation and longterm maintenance of landscaped areas within all forms of development. They ensure that planting and landscape works respond appropriately to site conditions, local topography, and existing vegetation, and that they enhance the public domain and the environmental quality of the urban environment.

Objectives

  • Promote high quality landscape design as an integral component of the overall design of a development
  • Provide landscape design and plantings that are compatible with the site and locality
  • Ensure that any new development considers and maximises the protection of existing vegetation in the site planning, design, development, construction and operation of the development
  • Encourage the preservation of trees and vegetation that contribute to native flora and fauna habitat
  • To recognise the importance of establishing and maintaining habitat corridors as links between areas of existing remnant bushland
  • To ensure there is no net loss of remnant bushland across the LGA
  • To incorporate landscaping as a way of fostering environmental benefits such as mitigating the urban heat island effect, reducing flood impacts, increasing groundwater retention and improving air quality
  • To provide landscaping that connects good urban design and development with urban bushland, in particular areas of high biodiversity
  • To increase the number of native and indigenous plantings across Randwick city.

Weed trees

Trees species that are declared weeds under the Biosecurity Act 2015 for the Randwick LGA. must not be incorporated into any landscape plans and must be actively managed on any private land.

See Appendix B4-1 for a table of weed trees relevant to Randwick.

2.1. Vegetation Clearing Requiring a Permit

A permit from Council is required where:

  • the clearing is not for a purpose that requires development consent
  • the trees to be cleared are covered by the Council's Development Control Plan Preservation of Trees B5
  • the clearing is below the NSW Biodiversity Offsets Scheme threshold.

Clearing below the NSW Biodiversity Offsets Scheme threshold

The NSW Biodiversity Offsets Scheme threshold (BOS threshold) identifies when proposed vegetation clearing must be assessed under the under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 (NSW), rather than under Council's local tree and vegetation management controls.

Where proposed vegetation clearing does not exceed the BOS threshold, the clearing may be assessed under this DCP and Council's relevant controls, subject to compliance with all other applicable legislation , instead of just through council's tree/vegetation controls .

Where proposed clearing exceeds the BOS threshold, the Biodiversity Offsets Scheme applies and:

  • the application must be accompanied by a Biodiversity Development Assessment Report (BDAR) prepared in accordance with the Biodiversity Assessment Method (BAM); and
  • approval must be obtained in accordance with the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 (NSW).

Applicants should note that clearing above the BOS threshold is not assessed solely under Council controls and requires determination under the State biodiversity assessment framework.

Table 1 - clearing limits for lot size Biodiversity Offset Scheme threshold
Minimum Lot sizeArea of clearing
Less than 1 hectare0.25 hectare or more
Less than 40 hectares but not less than 1 hectare0.5 hectare or more
Less than 1,000 hectares but not less than 40 hectares1 hectare or more
1,000 hectares or more2 hectares or more

Threshold limits as specified under Section 7.2 of the Biodiversity Conservation Regulation 2017

Controls

  • In accordance with the State Environmental Planning Policy (Biodiversity and Conservation) 2021, development consent is required for clearing of vegetation that does not exceed the Biodiversity Offsets Scheme (BOS) threshold where identified by this DCP
  • The following as vegetation is declared by Council to require development consent for clearing:
  • vegetation on land identified as 'Biodiversity' on the Terrestrial Biodiversity Map in the RLEP
  • vegetation on land zoned C2 Environmental Conservations C2 under the RLEP
  • vegetation on l and identified as 'Biodiversity Habitat Corridor' in the SSROC Connected Corridors for Biodiversity map
  • This control does not apply to the removal of undesirable or environmental weed species as specified in the Appendix B4-1 in this DCP
  • This control does not apply to:
  • Land zoned a C1 National Park under the Randwick LEP
  • land under the ownership or care, control and management of Randwick City Council where vegetation management works are undertaken by or on behalf of Council
  • A permit cannot apply to the following unless Council is satisfied that the clearing is minor in nature, is required for maintenance purposes and will not result in adverse impacts on:
  • a heritage item
  • a heritage conservation area,
  • forms part of an Aboriginal object or
  • an Aboriginal place.

Note

Vegetation clearing permit

Once received by Council a permit must be determined within 28 days after the date on which the application was duly made. If not determined is taken to have been refused after the expiration of that 28-day period

Development consent (via a Development Application) is required for clearing of vegetation (where development requires consent under Part 4 of the EP&A Act).

3. Landscape plan

Explanation

A landscape plan is required to accompany all DAs for new buildings, and significant alterations or additions that may affect existing vegetation, tree coverage or landscaped areas on the site. This requirement ensures that:

  • proposed developments contribute positively to the local environment and desired future character of the area
  • Retains and protects significant vegetation
  • supports urban biodiversity and ecological function
  • Maintains and enhances the visual quality and environmental performance of the site and surrounding locality.

Landscape plans are to demonstrate how the development integrates with the surrounding landscape setting and responds to the site constraints and opportunities for preserving significant vegetation.

Objectives

  • Contribute positively to the desired future character of the area
  • Soften the built form, improve streetscape presentation, and integrate new development with its surroundings
  • Provide high quality private and communal open space that is functional, landscaped, and well-shaded
  • Retain and enhance existing vegetation and landscape features
  • Support urban canopy, biodiversity and climate resilience outcomes.

Controls

  • A landscape plan submitted with a DA must be prepared in accordance with Appendix B4-3, including, but not limited to, the following elements and details:
  • Identification of all existing trees within or adjacent to the site including those on Council land. The plan must detail the location, height, condition and status of each tree (i.e. proposed to be removed/retained/relocated or pruned)
  • Documentation of existing natural and built site features such as rocky outcrops, cliff lines, water bodies, sandstone retaining walls and any other significant landscape elements
  • Delineation of hard and soft landscaped areas including deep soil zones and relationship of landscaped areas to buildings, accessways and open space areas
  • Location and selection of proposed plant species, including botanical and common names. Selection of species appropriate to site conditions and local character, with preference for locally indigenous or climate-adapted species
  • Location of drainage infrastructure, including pits and stormwater lines, irrigation systems, hose taps, and lighting proposed within landscaped areas
  • measures to manage stormwater, irrigation, erosion and sedimentation during and after construction, consistent with Council's Construction Water Management requirements as provided in Section 3.3 of Part B8 Water Management section of the DCP
  • Development consent must not be granted unless the consent authority is satisfied that the landscape design:
  • retains significant vegetation where feasible and minimises vegetation loss
  • provides adequate deep soil areas and planting to support canopy growth
  • integrates with the streetscape and surrounding landscape character
  • will achieve a high-quality, sustainable landscape outcome over the long term.

Notes

Appendix B4-3 outlines the requirements for Landscape Plans submitted with development applications.

Street verges - commercial, coastal and special precincts

Council's Urban Design Elements Manual (UDEM) applies to public domain upgrades in commercial centres, coastal areas, parks and special precincts. This Manual is available on Council's website.

Conditions of consent may require applicants to prepare, submit, and have approved by Council's Officers, detailed landscape plans which include plant schedules, planting plans, sample/materials boards and sections/elevations.

Where a contributions plan or a VPA agreement with Council applies (such as a Community Infrastructure Plan or a s.7.12 Development Contributions Plan), Council may consider public domain improvement works are delivered as 'works in kind' by a developer or through a monetary contribution to Council to undertake the work.

Street verges - residential areas

Council encourages the establishment of street gardens in residential street verges as part of development proposals rather than providing a standard turfed verge. Street gardens must be designed in accordance with Council's Street Garden Guidelines.

For larger developments, Council may require the applicant to upgrade the public verge with mass-planted, low growing, low maintenance species, consistent with the Street Garden Guidelines to support high-quality presentation and integration of new development into a residential streetscape. Such treatments improve landscape cohesion, increase shade potential and support Council's broader environmental, walkability and liveability objectives.

All public domain works are at the applicant's cost.

4. Landscape design

Explanation

The design of landscaped areas and deep soil planting constitutes an integral component of the overall site planning for any development. Accordingly, controls relating to the location, extent and design of landscaped areas and deep soil zones are provided within the relevant sections of this Development Control Plan (DCP) applicable for different development types, including:

  • C1 Low density residential
  • C2 Medium density residential
  • Part D4 Local centres
  • C10 Industrial uses
  • Part D15 Specific sites

4.1. Trees on development sites

Explanation

Development must be designed to retain and protect the urban forest values of the site by avoiding or minimising impacts on existing trees and providing appropriate replacement planting where tree removal is proposed. This requirement applies to all trees that may be affected by development, including those located on the site, within the public domain (Council owned trees) and on adjoining land. The retention and integration of existing vegetation is essential to maintaining canopy cover, supporting biodiversity and preserving the landscape character of the locality.

Objectives

  • Retain existing trees on development sites as an integral component of site planning
  • Increase canopy cover in accordance with Randwick's tree canopy target
  • Protect existing trees on development sites, adjoining properties or street trees in accordance with Australian Standard - AS 4970 - 2009 - Protection of Trees on Development Sites
  • Ensure development does not adversely impact trees on adjoining land or within the public domain.

Controls

  • Development must be designed to enable the retention of existing trees, including trees on adjoining land
  • Buildings, structures and excavation must be located outside the Tree Protection Zone (TPZ) of trees to be retained (whether on the site or on adjoining land), in accordance with AS4970 -Protection of trees
  • A Tree Protection Zone must be established and maintained for all existing trees to be retained prior to the commencement of any demolition or construction works
  • The following activities are not permitted within the TPZ:
  • Stockpiling of materials
  • No parking of any vehicles
  • Excavation, trenching or soil disturbance
  • Changes to soil levels
  • Trees on public land must be protected during demolition, excavation and construction work, through the installation of protective fencing or hoarding in accordance with Section 4 of AS4970-2009
  • Council will require the payment of a security deposit to ensure protection of trees on public land where:
  • Development is proposed within the Tree Protection Zone; or
  • Council determines that the development has the potential to impact the root zone, trunk or canopy of any tree.
  • Developments in zones other than R1 - General Residential or R2 - Low Density Residential must consider opportunities to
  • Underground overhead electrical services
  • Utilise aerial bundled cabling to minimise ongoing impacts on the tree canopy
  • New awnings, balconies or structures projecting over public land must be designed to accommodate existing street trees and allow for the establishment and future growth of street trees

Where tree removal is approved, replacement planting must be provided to:

  • Achieve canopy replacement appropriate to the scale and species of trees removed
  • Contribute to the long-term urban canopy of the locality.

4.2. Existing vegetation and natural features

Explanation

Significant natural features and vegetation contribute to the ecological function, landscape character and visual identity of a site and its surrounding area. These elements -including rocky outcrops, cliff lines, water bodies, trees, shrubs and groundcover vegetation should be retained and incorporated into the landscape design of the development.

Objectives

  • Conserve, protect and integrate significant natural features and vegetation into the design of development
  • Ensure site planning responds sensitively to the natural landform, supports ecological values including habitat, soil stability and water systems
  • Reinforces the visual and environmental character of the locality through landscaped-led design.

Controls

  • Development must be designed to avoid and minimise impacts on existing vegetation including trees, shrubs and groundcover vegetation
  • Retain and protect existing natural features as landscape elements within the site including water bodies, sandstone and rock outcrops and cliff lines and incorporate as part of the landscape design to inform the siting, orientation and form of development
  • Development must be designed to respond to natural landform and avoid excessive excavation, filling or regrading that would alter the site's natural character
  • Topsoil must be retained and stockpiled onsite where practicable for reuse in landscaped areas to support vegetation establishment.

4.3. Selection and location of plant species

Explanation

The appropriate selection and placement of plant species is essential to achieving high standards of landscape design, enhancing residential amenity, and supporting biodiversity conservation. Well-considered planting contributes to habitat creation, urban cooling, and the overall character of the development and surrounding area.

Objectives

  • Encourage the planting of appropriate native and locally indigenous plant species support and enhance habitat for fauna and flora
  • Ensure plant species are suited to the site's aspect, soil conditions and microclimate
  • Promote the use of local provenance/native species adapted to local conditions
  • Enhance the appearance and amenity of development through high quality planting design, selection and placement
  • Support Council's urban tree canopy targets by maximising canopy tree planting across the LGA
  • Increase the diversity and resilience of locally indigenous plant communities across the LGA.

Controls

  • A minimum of 60% of all plant species within the landscape plan must comprise native species, including a mix of locally indigenous trees, shrubs and groundcovers selected from Appendix B4-2
  • For the purposes of this control:
  • Cultivars or hybrids of listed plant species are not counted towards the minimum native planting requirement; and
  • The landscape plan must include a planting schedule that lists all proposed plant species, quantities and identifying species included in Appendix B42-1.
  • Invasive p lant species, and any species listed in Council's Undesirable Weed Species List Appendix B4-1 must not be included in the landscape design
  • This control may be varied for heritage-listed properties or heritage conservation areas where it can be demonstrated that the species is required to maintain the historic or cultural landscape character of the site
  • Plant selection and layout must enhance and extend existing fauna and flora habitats and contribute to ecological connectivity across the site and surrounding locality. Species selection should utilise Council's Native planting List Appendix B4-2, where appropriate
  • Where appropriate, development should incorporate food-growing areas (e.g. edible gardens, communal planting spaces) into the landscape design to support local sustainability and community wellbeing
  • Select and locate plants to improve environmental performance and site amenity. This includes:
  • Planting deciduous shade trees to regulate solar access - providing summer shade and allowing winter sunlight
  • Using vegetation to reduce glare from hard surfaces
  • Channelling air currents to improve natural ventilation
  • Providing wind buffering where appropriate; and
  • Use of vegetation to screen noise, enhance privacy, and reduce visual impacts.
  • Trees must be located to allow for mature growth and to minimise conflict with built structures and services. As a minimum, trees must be planted no closer than 3.5 metres

to the external wall of a building and trees must be located at least two (2) metres from any proposed or existing drainage infrastructure

  • Where a tree proposed for removal under a Development Application is three (3) metres or more in height or has a canopy spread of three (3) metres or more, replacement planting must be provided on a site
  • Replacement trees must:
  • Achieve a mature canopy size equal to or greater than that of the tree to be removed
  • Be specified and supported by a Landscape Plan and Arborist Report
  • Be selected from Council's Desirable Species List
  • Be planted as advanced stock from a minimum 45L pot size to support successful establishment.
  • Where, in Council's opinion, there is insufficient space on site to accommodate replacement trees of an appropriate size, the applicant may seek to contribute to offset planting on public land. Generally, for each tree removed, a minimum ratio of three (3) replacement trees for each tree removed is to be planted in accordance with Council's policy
  • Development must provide at least one (1) canopy tree within the property boundary where practicable. Where it is demonstrated that this requirement cannot be achieved due to the site constraints, a compensatory planting contribution or bond must be provided to support tree planting within the local area, in accordance with Council policy.

Notes:

Refer to Appendix B4-1of this DCP Section for a list of undesirable species.

A selection of native species may be available at Council's Nursery - stock list

Council's Native Havens Manual provides a list of native species suitable to various conditions

The Grow What Where Book provides information on native plants for a variety of settings, including unusual conditions or problem areas.

Local Provenance Plants

'Local provenance plants' are native species grown from seed or propagation material that has been collected from natural populations within the same local bioregion or ecological community as the development site. The use of local provenance ensures that plantings retain the genetic integrity and adaptive characteristics of local populations, thereby supporting long-term ecosystem resilience, habitat values, and biodiversity conservation.

As per control C2 Cultivars or Hybrid plants should not be planted near remnant bushland because they can compromise the ecological and genetic integrity of native plant populations. Hybrid plants may cross-pollinate with wild native species, leading to genetic contamination and a loss of locally adapted genetic traits that are critical for long-term survival in local conditions.

Appendix B4-2 provides a list of suitable native tree, shrub and groundcover species.

Contribution fees for public tree planting

Contribution fees for public tree planting in lieu of on-site replacement planting are set out in Council's Fees and Charges schedule.

4.4. Water efficient Landscaping

Explanation

High quality landscaping plays a critical role in influencing both the quality and quantity of stormwater runoff from a site, as well as the amount of water required for irrigation. Water efficient landscaping reduces potable water use, improves stormwater management and urban cooling and biodiversity outcomes.

For residential development, such measures assist in achieving BASIX water conservation targets. For non-residential development, they support broader water conservation and integrated water management outcomes consistent with Part B8- Water Management.

Objectives

  • Minimise potable (mains) water consumption for landscape irrigation.
  • Reduce stormwater runoff and improve on-site infiltration through effective landscape design and plant selection.
  • Promote drought-resilient and climate-responsive planting
  • Ensure landscape design contributes to integrated water cycle management

Controls

  • Development must be designed to maximise rainfall infiltration and minimise runoff, by:
  • reducing the extent of impervious surfaces
  • directing overland flow to permeable areas such as garden beds in line with the requirements of Part B8 - Water management
  • using semi-pervious materials for paved surfaces
  • Plant species must be selected to have low water requirements once established, be suited to local climatic and soil conditions and include deep rooted species to improve soil stability and drought resilience
  • Development should avoid extensive lawn areas, which typically require more water and fertiliser than native groundcovers, shrubs, and trees
  • Lawns will only be considered in rear yards of detached dwellings. Alternative low wateruse native groundcovers should be used in all other areas to enhance water efficiency and visual amenity
  • Water features must utilise recirculating systems and operate using non-potable water sources
  • Irrigation systems must be water efficient such as automated sub-soil drip systems such as soil moisture and rain sensors, and
  • use non-potable water sources (e.g. rainwater tanks)
  • Landscape design must incorporate water conservation practices including:
  • hydro zoning (grouping plants with similar water needs)
  • providing adequate soil depth to support water retention, plant health and reduced irrigation demand.

4.5. Minimum soil depth for landscaping

Objectives

  • Ensure landscaped areas provide adequate soil depth and volume to support healthy, vigorous and long term sustainable plant growth
  • Maximise canopy tree establishment, urban greening, and habitat creation through appropriate soil design and profiles
  • Enhance environmental performance by facilitating stormwater infiltration, reducing the urban heat island effect, and supporting local biodiversity
  • Contribute positively contribute to the visual amenity and character of the development and surrounding public domain through high quality landscaping.

Controls

  • Development must provide sufficient soil depth and volume to support healthy plant growth, canopy tree establishment, and long-term viability of landscaped areas
  • Soil depths and soil volume must be provided in accordance with the minimum requirements set out in Table 2
  • Where landscaping is located over structure (e.g., podiums, basements, roofs), a minimum soil depth of 1,000 mm for trees and 600 mm for shrubs must be provided, with appropriate drainage and irrigation.

Medium Trees (3-8m800mm2,000L per tree

4.6. Outdoor car parks & circulation areas

Explanation

Landscaping is an integral component of outdoor (at-grade) parking design. Well-designed landscape treatment offers a variety of benefits, including shade for parked vehicles, screening the car parks to reduce visual dominance, improve microclimatic conditions and contribute to urban tree canopy targets. Landscaping within open car parks also plays a key role in water sensitive urban design (WSUD), reducing stormwater runoff and mitigating urban heat island effects.

Objectives

  • Ensure outdoor ground level car parking areas are landscaped to provide effective shade and improve user comfort
  • Minimise the visual impact of car parking within the streetscape and public domain
  • Ensure that land uses requiring at-grade car parking, such as industrial and business park uses, incorporate adequate landscaping and vegetation to improve canopy cover reduce large areas of paved surfaces and minimise the urban heat island effects
  • Ensure landscaping is functional and does not compromise visibility or accessibility.

Controls

  • Outdoor ground level car parks containing 5 or more car spaces must incorporate landscape planting
  • Where landscaping is required, it must be designed in accordance with the following criteria:
  • Planting should be provided along the perimeter to screen car parking from streets and integrate with existing streetscape
  • Incorporate internal planting to break up large expanses of paving and provide shade to parked vehicles
  • Planting should maintain clear sightlines for both drivers and pedestrians, in accordance with relevant safety and CPTED principles
  • Internal planting should achieve a canopy tree planting rate of at least 1 tree per 4 car spaces or demonstrate an equivalent outcome capable of achieving a minimum50% canopy coverage of the car park at maturity
  • Planter beds must provide sufficient size and configuration to support long term tree growth, including adequate soil volume, depth, drainage and aeration, be protected from vehicle encroachment through kerbing or appropriate barriers and be designed to accommodate infiltration
  • Trees installed within car parks must have a minimum container size of 100 Litres at the time of planting
  • The following plant species should be used for car parks:
  • Trees with tall trunks and ample shade coverage
  • Plants that do not drop fruits, branches, sap or bark
  • Plants of vigorous growth and with minimum long-term maintenance requirements
  • Landscaping must be coordinated with site infrastructure ensuring appropriate clearances from planting and lighting, above ground electricity lines, footpaths, kerbs and underground services, etc.
  • Contrasting materials and finishes, including permeable paving, must be used to break up large sections of paving and to delineate pedestrian areas/crossings, entries, car parks, special use areas or at transition zones between different uses
  • Permeable paving surfaces must be prioritised for driveways, car parking bays and paved areas rather than non-permeable surfaces
  • Development involving 5 or more at grade car spaces must incorporate Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD) measures, including on-site stormwater infiltration through landscaped areas or bio-retention systems; and reduction of stormwater runoff generated by impervious surfaces.

5. Green roofs and green walls

5.1. Green roofs

Explanation

Green roofs comprise roof surfaces that are partially or fully vegetated and designed as integrated landscape systems. They can improve the building performance, reduce visual bulk when viewed from surrounding development and contribute to urban greening outcomes.

Green roofs provide multiple environmental benefits, including improved thermal performance, reduced stormwater run-off, increased biodiversity and mitigation of urban heat island effects. Green roofs offer a good option for renovating and improving the amenity of existing buildings where opportunities for at grade landscaping are limited.

A green roof system typically includes a waterproofing membrane and root barrier system, drainage system, filter fabric, a lightweight growing medium and vegetation.

Where appropriately designed, green roofs may contribute to landscape provision; however, their suitability and extent will be assessed by Council on a merit basis, having regard to functionality, accessibility, and long-term performance. Early consultation with Council is encouraged for proposals incorporating green roofs.

Objective

  • To encourage high quality, well designed and functional green roofs in suitable buildings and locations
  • To enhance urban greening, biodiversity and environmental performance in highly urbanised areas to achieve an appropriate quantity of landscape area
  • To provide additional useable or visual landscape space for urban greening, food production and useable private open space for residents.

Controls

  • Green roofs must be designed as an integrated building and landscape system, having regard to:
  • site conditions, including solar access, wind exposure and microclimate
  • the structural capacity, age and condition of the building
  • the intended function of the green roof (e.g. intensive, extensive, accessible or nonaccessible
  • Development applications incorporating a green roof must include a detailed site documentation demonstrating:
  • the site suitability, including consideration of the climate conditions (e.g. solar orientation and wind loads)
  • the depth and composition of the growing medium
  • planting design and species selection
  • the structural capacity of the building, age and condition of the roof
  • Select native and drought/heat tolerant plant species suited to roof conditions including high wind exposure, solar radiation and limited soil depths in accordance with Council's native species list as provided in Appendix B4-2. Other species may be considered and approved by Council's landscape officers
  • Be designed with high standard components, including waterproofing membrane, growing medium, vegetation layer, root barrier, insulation and drainage system
  • Green roofs must be designed to maximise retention and reuse of stormwater
  • Identify the most suitable irrigation system based on growing medium characteristics and plant needs
  • Green roofs should be designed to enable co-location with other rooftop uses where compatible, including solar photovoltaic systems
  • A maintenance plan must be submitted with the development application and must address at a minimum:
  • Inspection and maintenance of the waterproofing roof membrane
  • Drainage system performance and inspections
  • Ongoing care of plant health and replacement and
  • Maintenance of the irrigation system.

5.2. Green walls

Explanation

A green wall is a vertical vegetated system that may be, either free-standing or integrated into a building façade. Green walls can enhance the visual quality of development, reduce perceived building bulk and contribute to improved environmental performance.

Similar to green roofs, green walls can potentially offer a range of benefits, including lowering energy consumption through increased thermal performance, reduced noise transmission, improved air quality and enhanced urban biodiversity.

Green walls are considered supplementary landscaping measure and are not a substitute for required on-site landscaped area for any development.

Objectives

  • To encourage well designed, functional and maintainable green walls in appropriate locations
  • To promote ecologically sustainable design approaches for sites with constraints in highly urbanised contexts to achieve an appropriate quantity of landscape area
  • To enhance urban greening, building performance and environmental quality in dense urban areas.

Controls

Any development incorporating a green wall must:

  • Be designed and located to:
  • respond to the orientation, solar access, wind exposure and microclimatic conditions
  • provide safe and practical access for installation and ongoing maintenance.
  • Include a planting scheme that:
  • utilises species suited to vertical growing conditions and the specific microclimate
  • incorporate a mix of hardy, drought and heat tolerant species
  • prioritises native and ornamental species in accordance with Appendix B4-2 unless otherwise justified
  • Provide detailed design documentation demonstrating:
  • the structural support system
  • the growing medium and planting system
  • integration with the building structure and services
  • Be designed to ensure that:
  • the structural integrity and waterproofing of the building is not compromised
  • the system can be repaired, replaced or removed without damage to the building
  • Incorporate a water efficient irrigation system that:
  • is appropriate to the planting system and growing medium
  • includes automated controls (e.g. timers, soil moisture sensors)
  • utilises non-potable water sources where available
  • include a maintenance plan submitted with the development application that addresses:
  • irrigation system operation and monitoring
  • plant establishment, maintenance and replacement
  • inspection and upkeep of structural and support system.

6. Development and biodiversity

6.1. Development in or near areas of high biodiversity significance

Explanation

Areas of biodiversity significance in Randwick City are identified in the Terrestrial Biodiversity layer pursuant to the RLEP and are either zoned C2 Environment Conservation or identified in the SSROC connected corridors mapping. These identified sites are distributed across the City, including large areas of Eastern Suburbs Banksia Scrub (ESBS) and Acacia terminalis, listed as a critically endangered ecological community or species under the Biodiversity Conservation Act.

Biodiversity ValueSouth Sydney Region of Councils (SSROC) connected Corridors for BiodiversityDigital map link

Development within or adjacent to natural areas must be carefully planned and designed to avoid, minimise and mitigate impacts on biodiversity values at all stages of the development process

Council recognises the significant ecological value of remnant native vegetation and bushland, as well as the important habitat and biodiversity functions provided by revegetated areas. These areas are highly sensitive to urban encroachment and associated pressures, including fragmentation, edge effects, and increased human activity.

It is therefore essential that development responds appropriately to its context and incorporates measures to protect and enhance these natural assets, ensuring their long-term ecological integrity and resilience.

Note

In NSW the Biodiversity Offset Scheme (BOS) applies to development proposals under Part 4 of the EP&A Act that involve the clearing of native vegetation.

Local development will trigger the BOS if:

  • the proposed development footprint intersects land mapped on the Biodiversity Values Map (typically shown a shaded purple colour) or
  • The proposal exceeds the site area clearing threshold which varies depending on the minimum lot size associated with the site.

If either of these triggers is met the applicant must submit a Biodiversity Development Assessment Report (BDAR) with the Development Application.

The BDAR must

  • Be prepared in accordance with the NSW Biodiversity Assessment Method (BAM) Be completed by a NSW accredited assessor formally certified to apply the BAM and prepare BDARs

Objectives

The objectives for development in or near areas of high biodiversity value are to:

  • Protect existing biodiversity and habitat features within and adjacent to development sites
  • Ensure development in or adjacent to areas of biodiversity significance is designed, constructed and operated to appropriately manage the interface between the natural landscape and urban environment and protect the significant fauna and flora habitats
  • Maintain and enhance ecological function and connectivity
  • Protect and promote the recovery of threatened species, populations, and endangered ecological communities
  • Ensure development has regard for direct and indirect impacts on biodiversity and natural areas
  • Ensure landscape design elements are incorporated to provide a range of habitat features that can improve urban habitat
  • Protect, regenerate and conserve the local threatened ecological communities
  • Reduce the adverse impacts of light pollution on local fauna.

Controls

Development (including landscape works) within, or within 20m of areas of high biodiversity significance:

  • Must not impact on the environmental processes of natural areas, such as:
  • erosion of soils
  • siltation of streams and waterways
  • overland flows and stormwater runoff
  • overshadowing
  • removal or degradation of existing vegetation.
  • Must consider and undertake appropriate protective measures during the design, construction and operation phases, such as:
  • adequate buffer areas between any building structures and the natural areas
  • ongoing management arrangements to control invasive species and maintain natural features
  • silt/protective fencing
  • erosion and run off controls
  • appropriate site access points to prevent offsite disturbances
  • Landscape planting must prioritise native species with:
  • A minimum of 80% of the proposed trees
  • 90% of the proposed shrubs
  • 80% of the proposed grasses and groundcovers (not including turfed areas)
  • to be endemic or native species suited to the local ecological context.
  • Plant species selection must demonstrate that proposed landscaping will:
  • not directly or indirectly adversely affect the ecological functioning of nearby remnant bushland areas, including through the introduction of invasive species, creation of monocultures, or disruption to local hydrology or light regimes (affect the local native gene pool)
  • maintain the integrity of the local native gene pool, including through the use of locally appropriate species where practicable
  • enhance ecological, cultural and visual values, including by contributing to habitat connectivity and strengthening links between bushland areas.
  • Trees containing hollows must be retained wherever possible to support habitat for arboreal fauna. Consideration must be given to the potential risk of damage to public or private property as determined by a suitably qualified arborist
  • Where retention of hollow-bearing trees is proposed, an assessment prepared by a suitably qualified arborist must:
  • confirm the health and structural stability of the tree
  • identify and appropriately manage any risks to public safety or property.
  • Sites that are undeveloped should be protected and managed to encourage natural regeneration of native vegetation, including from the existing soil seed bank
  • External lighting on sites adjoining remnant vegetation must be designed and installed to minimise impacts on ecological values by:
  • directing light downwards and away from bushland, parks and reserves
  • minimising light spill, glare and reflective surfaces into parks, reserves and bushland
  • avoiding the short wavelength (blue-violet) light.

Note

Appendix B4-3 provides a list of suitable native tree, shrub and groundcover species.

Light Pollution impacts on Australia's wildlife can be minimised by considering light fixtures which have minimal impacts upon wildlife as outlined in the National Light Pollution Guidelines for Wildlife (dcceew.gov.au)

7. Penalties

Clearing of vegetation that is not carried out in accordance with a valid development consent or is not exempt under relevant planning controls will be dealt with in accordance with the relevant legislation set out below.

Local Government Act 1993 Under Section 629 of the Local Government Act (NSW) addresses the protection of public places by prohibiting the wilful or negligent injury, damage, or disturbance of plants, animals, rocks, or soil in such areas. Penalties may apply to the injury or unnecessary disturbance of any plant, animal, rock or soil from a public place.

Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 Under Sections 9.50 and 9.51 of the court action (in addition to any pecuniary penalty) may apply to the destruction of or damage to a tree or vegetation. Offenders may be required to rehabilitate the site, plant new trees and vegetation and maintain these until maturity.

Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 (NSW) and National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974 (NSW) - Additional penalties may apply where vegetation clearing impacts threatened species, ecological communities, or critical habitat. These offences may attract significant fines and, in serious cases, criminal prosecution.

Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 - Where clearing affects matters of national environmental significance (e.g. listed threatened species or migratory species), Commonwealth penalties may also apply.

Recent enforcement actions by the NSW Land and Environment Court have resulted in record fines exceeding $1 million for unlawful clearing, reflecting the seriousness with which these offences are treated

Councils and regulatory authorities are also empowered to issue stop work orders, remediation directions, and pursue legal action where necessary

Note

injury to a tree means but is not limited to: poisoning; spilling or washing off toxic chemicals; applying herbicides to a tree or within a Tree Protection Zone; damaging tree roots using stockpiling materials, soil compaction, filling, excavation or altering soil levels within Tree Protection Zone; wounding tree trunks or the breaking or tearing of roots or branches; wounding trunks or branches by fixing objects using nails, wires, staples or similar fastening materials e.g. attaching signs, swings, platforms or cubby houses.

Appendix B4-3: Landscape plan requirements

  • The Landscape Plan must be prepared by a suitable qualified and experienced landscape architect
  • Plans must be drawn at a scale not less than 1:100
  • The plan must demonstrate a clear understanding of the site and its environmental context, including consideration of local conditions such as sandy soils and coastal influences
  • The plan must be prepared in accordance with Part 3 Landscape Design of this DCP
  • The Plan must include a plant species list, detailing the botanical and common names of plants, pot sizes, quantity of each species and area of origin (native, endemic, exotic)
  • For properties containing or adjoining remnant vegetation, habitat corridors or areas recognised ecological significance (as identified in Section 8- Development in or near areas of high biodiversity significance) the landscape plan must align with the provisions of Section 5 of this DCP
  • The Plan must clearly identify all proposed changes to landscaped areas including:
  • Existing levels and finished levels (indicating the extent of cut and fill)
  • Provision of deep soil areas (minimum depth of 400mm)
  • Retention of existing landscaping
  • Trees proposed for removal
  • Details of proposed new planting (species, pot size, mature height, and quantity)
  • Proposed surface treatments (e.g. turf, paving, etc.).

Appendix B4-4: Guidelines for arborists ' reports

Where necessary, Council will require an arborist to prepare a tree/vegetation report and the minimum accepted qualification for an arborist is the Australian Qualification Framework level 4 (AQF4).

Where trees are listed on Council's Register of Significant Trees, a report must be prepared by a qualified arborist. The minimum accepted qualification for a qualified arborist is the Australian Qualification Framework level 5 (Diploma) (AQF5).

The following information is required to be included in any Arborists ' Report:

  • Name, address, telephone number, ABN, qualifications and experience of the arborist who inspected the tree/s and prepared the report
  • Address of the site, where the tree/s are located
  • Who the report was prepared for, date site inspected, date report prepared and the aims of the report
  • Methods and/or techniques used in the inspection
  • A plan (to scale) accurately showing:
  • location of tree/s on the subject site and any adjoining trees which may be affected by any development. Trees identified on the plan shall be named and numbered
  • optimum and minimum tree protection zones - if recommended by the arborist
  • lot boundaries, dimensions and North point
  • proposed development including services, driveways and any alteration to existing and proposed soil levels and drainage, as well as distances (in mm) between tree/s and works
  • A table showing, for each tree to be pruned/removed:
  • number of the tree - as indicated in the plan
  • species name
  • conservation status (whether or not is a threatened species or a component of Endangered Ecological Community)
  • age class
  • height
  • canopy width
  • trunk circumference at one (1) metre above ground level
  • health and condition, and estimated Safe Useful Life Expectancy
  • A discussion of other relevant information, including details of tree hollows for wildlife, tree structure/defects, root form and distribution, pests and diseases and/or a Tree Hazard Assessment
  • Supporting evidence such as photographs and laboratory results to confirm the presence of soil pathogens or to support soil assessment, where relevant
  • Proposed replacement plantings, landscaping and/or soil remediation
  • Tree protection measures and a post-construction tree maintenance program which can be used as development consent conditions, should the application be approved
  • Sources of information referred to in the report
  • Measures to minimise impacts of proposed/approved development - e.g., footing designs, excavation techniques, vents to atmosphere, etc.
  • Any other relevant matters or information such as Resistograph or Picus Sonic Tomograph reports.

Qualified arborists and their contact details may be obtained from the Institute of Australian Consulting Arboriculturists (IACA) (www.iaca.org.au) or from Arboriculture Australia (www.arboriculture.org.au).

These organisations are not specifically recommended and Council will accept arborist's reports from any registered member of a nationally recognised arboriculturally organisation or association.

1. Introduction

A healthy urban forest provides significant aesthetic, ecological and environmental benefits to residents, workers and visitors of Randwick City. It is of vital importance to protect and enhance the City's urban environment through long term preservation a nd management of trees and other vegetation in our urban forest. Preserving the City's tree coverage is important in protecting the liveability of our neighbourhoods. As a large proportion of the City's tree canopy is existing on private land, observance of Council's tree and vegetation controls are imperative to protec t our city's trees and vegetation.

Implementing the Green Grid, protecting areas of bushland and biodiversity, increasing tree canopy cover and increasing the native and indigenous species across the LGA are key priorities of the City of Randwick Environmental Strategy 2022 and our Local Strategic Planning Statement 2036.

This section applies to trees in Randwick City and supplements the State Environmental Planning Policy Biodiversity and Conservation 2021 (BC SEPP) by specifying additional types of tree works which require Council approval and guidance for preparation of applications seeking Council Tree permit approval.

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

  • Part B4 Landscaping and Biodiversity of the DCP which covers trees on development sites.

Tree removal that is associated with building work requiring consent will be evaluated as part of the development assessment process and may also require additional assessment and approval under the NSW Biodiversity Act (2016). Please see Part B4 - Landscaping and Biodiversity . If you wish to remove a tree or trees that have been conditioned to be retained or forms part of the approved landscape design in a development consent, you are required to apply for a section 4.55 or 4.56 amendment to your development consent.

Alignment with other planning instruments

In addition to the Randwick Local Environment Plan (LEP), the Biodiversity Conservation SEPP applies.

In the event of an inconsistency between this DCP and the SEPP, the SEPP prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.

Other Council documents

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with the following tree management documents, which can be found on Council's website:

  • Tree Management Technical Manual
  • Significant Tree Register
  • Urban Forest Policy
  • Sewerage Stormwater Drain Blockage Policy
  • Street Tree Masterplan
  • Street Tree Identification Manual
  • Randwick City Council Local Environment Plan

2. Tree Permits

Objectives

The specific aims of this section are:

  • To effectively protect and enhance the urban forest in Randwick City Council
  • To protect and retain trees with cultural, heritage and natural significance
  • To provide effective tree protection measures that promote the retention of vegetation and increase tree canopy coverage across the City of Randwick.

Controls

  • A tree permit is required to clear or carry out tree works to any of the following:
  • Any hollow bearing trees
  • Severing of tree roots greater than 50 mm
  • Tree with a height equal to or exceeding 5 metres
  • Tree with a canopy width equal to or exceeding 4 metres
  • For a single trunk tree species, a trunk circumference equal to or exceeding 400 mm at a height of one (1) metre above ground level
  • For a multi-trunk tree species, a combined trunk circumference (measured around the outer girth of the group of trunks) equal to or exceeding 400 mm at a height of one (1) metre above ground level.

Note

Unless specifically exempt under this Plan or other applicable legislation, the pruning, damaging, or removal of any of the prescribed trees listed above must not occur without prior written consent from Council. Such consent is to be obtained through either a Tree Permit Application or a Development Application for Tree Works, as determined by the tree's location and relevant planning controls.

An arboriculture assessment (Arborist) report by a suitably qualified Australian Qualification Framework (AQF) Level 5 Arborist, and other specialist reports and information may be required to be submitted as part of the application/permit assessment process as evidence to support the pruning or removal of the tree(s).

Relevant forms are 'Application for Permit to Prune/Remove Tree/s' and 'DA for Tree Works'. Both can be downloaded from Council's website

https://www.randwick.nsw.gov.au/environment-and-sustainability/trees/removing-andpruning-trees

3. Development Applications for Tree Works

Objectives

  • To ensure the protection and appropriate management of trees with heritage, cultural, or significant value by establishing clear requirements for Development Applications involving pruning or removal, thereby safeguarding the historic, cultural, and natural character of the area.

Controls

  • A Development Application (DA) for Tree Works is required to prune more than 10% of the live canopy within any 12-month period or to remove any tree that meets one or more of the following criteria:
  • The tree is located within a Heritage Conservation Area or forms part of a Heritage Item
  • The tree is, or forms part of, an Aboriginal object or is within an Aboriginal place of heritage significance
  • The tree is listed on Council's Register of Significant Trees

The proposed tree works will have an impact on heritage significance or amenity.

Note

All Development Applications for tree works must be lodged using Council's prescribed 'Development Application for Tree Works' form.

All trees listed on Council's Register of Significant Trees are considered to have historic, cultural and natural significance. The Register can be viewed at Council's website.

If approval is given for the pruning and removal of tree(s) as part of DA consent, tree works can only be carried out when construction work physically and substantially commences.

Branches must not exceed 40mm in diameter for each pruning occurrence. Pruning work is to be carried out in accordance with Australian Standard AS 4373 - 2007 - Pruning of Amenity Trees

4. Exempt Vegetation

Objectives

  • To clearly define circumstances where tree pruning or removal may occur without Council consent/permit, ensuring works are limited to essential maintenance, safety, and statutory obligations, and are carried out in accordance with recognised standards to protect environmental and heritage values.

Controls

  • Council consent is not required for tree works that meet all the following conditions:
  • All pruning must comply with AS 4373 - 2007 Pruning of Amenity Trees
  • Trees certified by Council or a qualified arborist as posing an imminent risk to life or property
  • Emergency works undertaken under the State Emergency and Rescue Management Act 1989 or State Emergency Service Act 1989, with written verification (including photographs and an arborist's report) provided to Council within 6 months
  • Removal of trees confirmed as dead and not as the result of poisoning or vandalism or providing habitat for native fauna, with evidence retained
  • Removal of vegetation declared a priority weed under the Biosecurity Act 2015, except where located in a Heritage Conservation Area or are part of a heritage item, in which case Council must be notified at least 7 days prior (see Annexure B5-2 for a list of undesirable weed trees)
  • Selective pruning of branches up to 40mm diameter within 2m of a building (work is in accordance with Australian Standard AS 4373 - 2007 - Pruning of Amenity Trees)
  • Crown thinning limited to 10% of live canopy within any 2 year period
  • Removal of deadwood over 50mm diameter, roots under 50mm diameter, or branches up to 2.5m above ground level
  • Formative pruning for young tree for powerline clearance in accordance with AS 4373 - 2007 Pruning of Amenity Trees and relevant utility guidelines
  • Tree works to give effect to a development consent that permits the pruning or removal of the tree/s
  • Any works authorised by or under the State Emergency and Rescue Management Act 1989 or State Emergency Service Act 1989 in relation to an emergency (within the meaning of that Act) and that was reasonably necessary to avoid an actual or imminent threat to life or property; and any emergency firefighting act or bush fire hazard reduction work within the meaning of the Rural Fires Act 1997 that is authorised or required to be carried out under that Act.
  • The exemptions do not apply to:
  • Tree/s that are required to be retained by a condition of development consent
  • Trees on public land owned or managed by Council
  • Tree/s required to be planted as a condition of development consent or condition in a tree permit
  • Threatened species or land containing native vegetation (including dead trees) that provides habitat for threatened species, populations, or ecological communities listed under Schedules 1 and 2 of the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016, as well as other protected matters under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Commonwealth)
  • Land that is a declared area of outstanding biodiversity value under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016
  • Land declared critical habitat under Part 7A of the Fisheries Management Act 1994
  • Any native prescribed tree located as described in Section B4 areas of High Biodiversity Value
  • Pruning more than 10% of the canopy, or proposed removal of a prescribed tree that is a heritage item, forms part of a Local heritage item, or is listed in the significant tree register, or located in a Local heritage conservation area or where the tree forms part of an Aboriginal object or is located within an Aboriginal place of heritage significance.

Note: written verification from a qualified person

Where a tree is removed because it is dead or poses an imminent risk to human life or property (e.g., following storm damage), the landowner must provide written verification to Council and retain this evidence for at least six (6) months after the event.

Such evidence should include:

  • Photographs clearly showing the tree's condition
  • A tree risk assessment from a AFQ Level 5 arborist identifying the risk to human life or property
  • A written statement from a qualified arborist confirming the tree's condition and that it does not provide habitat for protected species
  • A written statement from the State Emergency Service (SES), if works were carried out by SES at the owner's request.

Expert advice from an arborist must be obtained with respect to these trees to confirm their condition and that they do not provide habitat for protected species.

Cutting or removal of threatened species, endangered communities, or their habitats, which pose a threat to life and property, can only be authorised under:

  • State Emergency and Rescue Management Act 1989, or
  • State Emergency Service Act 1989.

Any other removal may breach the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974, attracting significant penalties.

5. Penalties

Any clearing, pruning, or removal of vegetation without a Vegetation Clearing Permit, not in accordance with a development consent, or not exempt under this Plan or relevant legislation will be subject to enforcement action under applicable laws. These include the Local Government Act 1993 and the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.

Local Government Act 1993 (Section 629)

It is an offence to wilfully or negligently injure, damage, or unnecessarily disturb any tree or vegetation in a public place, including road reserves. Maximum penalty: 20 penalty units.

Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 (Division 9.6)

Failure to obtain the required approval (development consent or tree permit, as applicable) constitutes an offence under Division 9.6. Offenders may be liable to:

Failure to obtain the required approval, (that is, development consent or tree permit as applicable) is an offence under the Division 9.6 Criminal offences and proceedings under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979. This will render persons liable to significant penalties, issue of a Penalty Notice and/or the issue of an Order by Council. Offenders may also be required to rehabilitate the site, plant new trees and vegetation and maintain these until maturity.

Note

For the purposes of this Plan, 'injure a tree' includes, but is not limited to:

  • Poisoning or applying herbicides to a tree or within its Tree Protection Zone (TPZ)
  • Spilling or washing off toxic chemicals within the TPZ
  • Damaging roots through stockpiling materials, soil compaction, excavation, filling, or altering soil levels within the TPZ
  • Wounding trunks or branches or breaking/tearing roots or branches
  • Fixing objects to trunks or branches using nails, wires, staples, or similar fasteners.

Note

A development application is required for pruning of more than 10% of a tree/s canopy or removal of a prescribed tree/s located on a property which is a heritage item, forms part of a heritage item, is listed in the heritage trees list, is located in a heritage conservation area or where the tree forms part of an Aboriginal object or is located within an Aboriginal place of heritage significance.

6. Effect of State Environmental Planning Policy (Exempt and Complying Development Codes)

The State Environmental Planning Policy (Exempt and Complying Development Codes) 2008 (Codes SEPP) contains provisions that affect tree and vegetation removal in relation to exempt and complying development. This section clarifies how these provisions apply within Randwick City.

Objectives

  • To ensure consistency between this DCP and the Codes SEPP regarding tree and vegetation removal
  • To prevent unauthorised removal of prescribed trees during exempt or complying development
  • To maintain heritage, environmental, and amenity values while facilitating lawful development.

Controls

Exempt Development

  • Under Clause 1.16(1)(b) of the Codes SEPP, development cannot be considered exempt if it involves:
  • The removal or pruning of any tree or vegetation that requires consent under this DCP or other legislation, unless carried out in accordance with a valid permit or development consent.

Complying Development

  • Under Clause 3.1(2) and related provisions of the Codes SEPP:
  • A Complying Development Certificate (CDC) must not be issued if the proposal involves removal or pruning of a prescribed tree without Council approval
  • Where tree removal is proposed, the applicant must provide:
  • A Tree Permit or relevant Development Consent from Council; and
  • Evidence that the tree is not listed on Council's Register of Significant Trees .
  • Tree works associated with complying development must comply with:
  • AS 4373 - 2007 Pruning of Amenity Trees; and
  • Any conditions imposed by Council in the permit or consent.
  • All vegetation located on Council land shall be protected in accordance with the relevant sections within Council's Tree Management Technical Manual. The tree protection measures shall be in place for the full duration of any work carried out through a CDC.

Distance and Size Restrictions

  • Vegetation less than 3m in height and located more than 3m from any building (other than an exempt structure) may be removed without consent, subject to compliance with this DCP and Codes SEPP
  • Trees within Heritage Conservation Areas, forming part of a Heritage Item, or listed on the Register of Significant Trees are not exempt under the Codes SEPP.

Heritage and Aboriginal Significance

  • Tree works affecting heritage significance or Aboriginal objects/places are not permitted as exempt or complying development under the Codes SEPP and require Council approval.

Note

Private Certifiers must ensure compliance with these provisions before issuing a Complying Development Certificate (CDC). Failure to obtain required approvals may result in enforcement action under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 and Local Government Act 1993.

Notes: State Environmental Planning Policy (Exempt and Complying Development Codes) 2008 If works are proposed under exempt development would involve cutting down or pruning a tree:

  • You must first obtain tree removal approval from council unless the tree is exempt as specified in Section 4.1 Exempt Vegetation.

For complying development, the certifier cannot issue a CDC (Complying Development Certificate) if the works would require removal of a prescribed tree without council approval.

State Environmental Planning Policy (Exempt and Complying Development Codes) 2008

1.16: General requirements for exempt development:

  • To be exempt development for the purposes of this Policy, the development must -

(b) not involve the removal or pruning of a tree or other vegetation that requires a permit, approval or development consent, unless the removal or pruning is carried out in accordance with the permit, approval or development consent

  • General requirements for complying development:
  • (h) for development involving the removal or pruning of a tree or other vegetation that requires a permit, approval or development consent - before the complying development certificate is issued, have the permit, approval or development consent.

3.33 Setbacks of dwelling houses attached development and detached development from protected trees:

(1) Pruning and removal of trees A complying development certificate for complying development under Division 1 is taken to satisfy any requirement under this Policy for a permit, approval or development consent to remove or prune a tree or other vegetation on the lot if -

  • (a) the tree is not listed on a register of significant trees kept by the council, and
  • (b) the tree or vegetation will be within 3m of any building that has an area of more than 25m2, and
  • (c) the tree or vegetation has a height that is less than -
  • for development that is the erection of a dwelling house - 8m and is not required to be retained as a condition of consent, or
  • in any other case - 6m.

Appendix A: Definitions

Dead tree means a tree with no living vascular tissue.

Destroy means any activity leading to the death, disfigurement or mutilation of a tree.

Height means the distance measured vertically between the horizontal plane of the lowest point of the base of the tree/s which is immediately above ground level and the horizontal plane of the uppermost point of the tree/s.

Injury or injuring means damage to a tree and includes:

  • Killing or destruction of a tree or
  • Removal of a tree without appropriate consent
  • Severing of branches, limbs, stems over 40mm, damage to the trunk and/or roots.
  • Lopping and topping.
  • Poisoning, including applying herbicides and other plant toxic chemicals to a tree or spilling (including washing off or directing water contaminated by) oil, petroleum, paint, cement, mortar and the like onto the root zone.
  • Cutting and tearing of branches and roots that is not carried out in accordance with accepted arboriculture practices, does not qualify as 'pruning' (as defined within AS 4373 - 2007 - Pruning of Amenity Trees ), or which is done for invalid reasons.
  • Ringbarking, scarring the bark when operating machinery, fixing objects (e.g., signs) by nails, staples or wire, using tree climbing spikes in healthy trees marked for retention (except for access to an injured tree worker) or fastening materials that circle and significantly restrict the normal vascular function of the trunk or branches.
  • Damaging a tree's root zone by compaction, excavation or asphyxiation (including unauthorised filling or stockpiling of materials).
  • Under scrubbing, particularly carried out by mechanical tools such as brush cutters and the like.

Imminent risk includes but is not restricted to obvious instability of the root system, evidence of soil heave or cracking, loss of structural roots, root decay, storm damage and structural defects that are imminently hazardous, such as splitting branches. Evidence must be provided to Council in writing by photographic evidence or written evidence by a Qualified Arborist (AQF5).

Lopping means the cutting of branches or stems between branch unions or at internodes on trees.

Dead tree means a tree with no living vascular tissue.

Prune or pruning means cutting branches from a tree/s in a planned and systematic manner that is carried out in accordance with the provisions of AS 4373 - 2007 - Pruning of Amenity Trees , and which consists of the following pruning types:

  • Crown maintenance pruning involving:
  • general pruning
  • thinning
  • dead wooding
  • selective pruning
  • formative pruning

(Crown maintenance pruning relates to pruning according to the growth habit of the tree/s without reducing the area of the crown, while retaining the structure and size of the tree/s.)

  • Crown modification pruning involving:
  • reduction pruning
  • crown lifting
  • pollarding
  • remedial pruning
  • powerline clearance

(Crown modification pruning relates to pruning that changes the structural appearance and habit of the tree/s.)

Remove or removal means to cut down, fell, destroy, kill, take away, uproot or transplant a tree from its place of origin.

Topping means cutting away part or all of the tree canopy, leaving a trunk and stubbed main branches.

Tree works are works affecting the form, structure or foliage of a tree including root cutting, crown lifting, reduction pruning, selective pruning, crown thinning, remedial or restorative pruning or complete tree removal.

Trunk means the main stem of the tree, as distinguished from the branches and roots.

Undesirable species are plants listed in this control which are deemed undesirable due to characteristics which may lead to poisoning, weed infestation or bushland invasion.

Width means the distance measured horizontally (in metres) between the two (2) widest points of a tree's canopy.

Appendix C: Assessment criteria for tree works

The following matters are considered, but not limited to

  • Whether the tree has significant amenity or aesthetic value or is ecologically significant, with particular emphasis placed on retaining trees listed on Council's Register of Significant Trees. The condition, maturity and Safe Useful Life Expectancy (SULE) of the tree/s
  • A report from a qualified arborist (AFQ 5 or higher), if required
  • Whether the tree is affected by the provisions of any other Act, Regulation or State Environmental Planning Policy applying to the land
  • The potential hazards to persons and/or property in the context of:
  • the structural soundness of the particular tree (including condition of the canopy, amount of deadwood, any prolonged decline, significant and sustained insect attack, etc); and/or
  • the characteristics and risk potential of the particular species; and/or
  • siting issues such as ground conditions, building proximity, etc, which may give rise to a hazardous situation (particularly structural damage to public infrastructure and/or private property caused by the tree/s, its trunk or its root system); and/or
  • ill health, such as allergies, where specific evidence is provided by an expert in the relevant medical field and a link between the ailment and the species is reasonably established; and/or
  • existing (or potential for) traffic obstruction in relation to proximity to a roadway, intersection or driveway, where pruning would be an insufficient remedy
  • Whether the proposed work needs to be carried out by a suitably qualified and experienced person
  • Whether the tree is mapped within the 'Biodiversity Habitat Corridor'
  • Whether appropriate additional (or replacement) planting has been or should be undertaken
  • The need for, and suitability of, soil erosion and siltation controls
  • Whether tree protection measures are required prior to works commencing
  • Whether a tree or vegetation is or provides habitat of a threatened species or ecological communities listed in Schedule 1 or 2 of the Biodiversity Conservation Act (BC Act) 2016
  • Whether, prior to the felling of a tree, special measures should be in place to reduce the potential for injury or death of animals likely to inhabit the tree. Such measures may include:
  • inspection of hollows and other potential habitat sites on the tree
  • sectional dismantling
  • supervision of works by an arborist and/or a licensed wildlife carer or handler
  • The following should not generally be considered as valid reasons to remove a tree/s or native vegetation:
  • leaf drop to gutters, downpipes, pools, lawns, etc.
  • to increase natural light, where it is the sole consideration
  • to improve street lighting into private property
  • to enhance views or reduce the height of trees
  • to reduce shade created by a tree/s - particularly species such as Ficus or Araucaria
  • to reduce fruit, resin or bird droppings falling onto driveways and/or cars
  • minor lifting of driveways, front fences, paths and footpaths by tree roots
  • to erect a fence
  • bushfire hazard control, which has not been verified by Council; or potential damage to sewer mains or stormwater pipes, unless supported by written expert advice and only where reasonable alternatives are not feasible (e.g. relocation or encasement of mains and replacement of damaged pipes in PVC plastic).
