1. Introduction

Explanation

Randwick City aspires to becoming a well-connected, climate-resilient community where transport infrastructure supports road safety, sustainable growth, equitable access, and vibrant urban life.

Over the next decade, the Local Government Area (LGA) will experience continued growth and development in its commercial centres and residential areas, necessitating the progressive improvement of the public transport network to further connect and support mode share options, and to facilitate the realisation of the 30-minute city concept - where residents live within convenient walking distance of employment, public transport, essential services and recreational opportunities.

The following provisions are designed to complement the objectives of the Randwick Local Environmental Plan (LEP), with a focus on fostering a well-connected, sustainable and inclusive urban environment. These provisions aim to:

  • Encourage an efficient and appropriate mix of land uses, vibrant centres, and seamless integration between land use and transport
  • Promote sustainable travel by prioritising safe walking, public transport and cycling use in line with Council's Transport Hierarchy
  • Ensure equitable access to transport infrastructure for people of all ages and abilities
  • Enhance urban liveability through safe, healthy and inclusive public spaces connected by active transport networks
  • Support diverse housing and employment opportunities through effective land use and transport connectivity
  • Align development aligns with climate resilience goals, including the reduction of transport-related emissions
  • As travel behaviour shifts towards low-emission modes, Randwick City will focus on delivering safe, legible, and integrated networks that connect people to places, strengthen local centres, and reflect the community's aspirations for a liveable, green and futureready city.

This Part of the DCP incorporates a range of initiatives that apply to all development in Randwick City. They outline objectives and controls that Development Applications (DA) must address through thoughtful design, and well managed access and parking arrangements. These controls encourage the adoption of alternative transport modes and supports a sustainable transport approach. It also specifies the types of supporting studies that may be required when lodging a development application.

This section of the DCP should be read in conjunction with:

  • Part A - Introduction
  • Part B - General Controls
  • Network Planning in Precincts Guide
  • Design of Roads and Streets (DORAS)
  • Road User Space Allocation Policy
  • Walking Space Guide
  • Walkable Public Space
  • Cycleway Design Toolbox (2020)
  • Movement and Place principles.
  • Other Parts of the DCP for specific development types, locations or sites, if relevant to the DA.

Note

DAs are to consider relevant guidance from the following documents, particularly in the context of improving urban design and sustainable transport opportunities:

1.1. Objectives

The overarching transport objectives are to:

  • Develop a transport network that prioritises active and public transport use as the preferred transport mode, by enhancing accessibility, connectivity and user amenity
  • Promote low-emission and shared transport options in both new and existing developments to reduce environmental impact and strengthen climate resilience
  • Restrict off-street parking provision in areas well-served by high-frequency public and active transport infrastructure to discourage private car dependency and reduce congestion
  • Encourage multimodal transport options for development, particularly along key transport corridors, within commercial centres and at strategic/key sites to improve accessibility, flexibility and user amenity
  • Support the integration of car share schemes, bicycle and scooter parking, and connections to public transport to enhance mobility and reduce congestion
  • Ensure car parking facilities, service and delivery areas, and access points are designed to complement and enhance the streetscape character and protect pedestrian amenity and safety
  • Limit vehicle access points along major transport corridors and regional roads to preserve traffic flow and enhance road safety.

2. Sustainable transport

2.1. Public and active transport

Explanation

Randwick City's public transport system is predominantly bus-based complemented by the South East Light Rail, which provides key connections to and from the Sydney CBD. Local and regional bus services also play a key role in connecting the local area to surrounding destinations, such as Bondi Junction, Waverley, Maroubra Beach, and Coogee Beach.

Access to public transport is essential for sustainable urban mobility. It relies not only on welllocated services but also on supporting infrastructure - such as bus and light rail stops, pedestrian crossings, bicycle paths, footpaths - that are safely and effectively integrated with pedestrian and cycling networks. Seamless connectivity between these elements is essential to ensure inclusive access for all users.

Walking and cycling, collectively referred to as active transport, represent the most sustainable modes of travel. They contribute to healthier lifestyles, cleaner environments and support vibrant public spaces. At the State level, the NSW Active Transport Strategy sets an ambitious goal to double the number of people walking and cycling in NSW over the next 20 years.

While acknowledging the continued need for car travel, this DCP promotes the transition toward more sustainable and integrated transport solutions. The NSW Government, through Transport for New South Wales (TfNSW) introduced the Electric and Hybrid Vehicle Plan aiming for net zero transport emissions by 2050 and investing in electric vehicle infrastructure and services.

Transport for NSW is also undertaking reforms to improve the operation and management of shared e-micromobility services such as shared e-bikes across New South Wales. These reforms aim to establish a clearer and more consistent regulatory framework that supports safe, accessible, and well-managed services for communities.

More information on e-micromobility can be found here:

https://www.nsw.gov.au/driving-boating-and-transport/bikes-e-bikes-e-scooters/emicromobility-action-plan

This DCP part supports active and sustainable transport initiatives by enhancing infrastructure for walking and cycling, encouraging the uptake of electric vehicles and facilitating the integration of these measures into new developments and the broader public transport network. The goal is to create a more connected, cleaner and future ready City.

Objectives

To promote sustainable transport by:

  • Integrating development with the broader public transport network
  • Encouraging the take up of sustainable transport modes including walking, cycling, and public transport.

Controls

  • All development must address transport, access and parking requirements by incorporating measures that increase the share of trips made by public transport, walking and cycling
  • Developments should include flexible hardstand areas to support bicycle maintenance and repair activities
  • Where a variation to the DCP Car Parking rates is proposed, proponents must respond directly to the provisions in Section 8 Exceptions to Parking Rates of this DCP
  • A Green Travel Plan (GTP) must accompany all DAs for new buildings and substantial alterations to existing buildings. The GTP is to include:
  • Mode share targets, aimed at reducing private car travel
  • Travel demand management strategies to encourage sustainable transport choices
  • Development proposals must include initiatives to implement and monitor travel measures such as car share and bike share programs
  • Development proposals must include provision for electric charging stations in accessible on-site locations.

2.2. Bicycles

Explanation

Environmentally sustainable, healthy and vibrant cities support alternative transport modes such as cycling, which require safe, well-designed infrastructure and connected bicycle routes.

Key activity generators within Randwick City- including the University of New South Wales, Randwick Hospitals Campus, Centennial Park and coastal destinations - create significant demand for non-car transport options. By improving facilities for cyclists and pedestrians there is an opportunity to reduce car dependency, promote active transport and enhance public health outcomes.

This section sets out bicycle parking requirements for various development types. Where a specific land use is not listed, a merit-based assessment will be applied to ensure bicycle parking is appropriately provided.

DAs requiring bicycle facilities must consider the following documents:

  • Australian Standard AS 2890.3 Parking Facilities - Part 3: Bicycle parking
  • Austroads Guide to Traffic Management - Bicycle Parking Facilities
  • Cycling Aspects of Austroads Guides (AP-G88-17)
  • TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment

Objectives

The objectives for on-site bicycle facilities are to:

  • Support active, healthy lifestyles through the provision of cycling infrastructure
  • Promote cycling as a safe, convenient and low emission mode of transport
  • Ensure equitable access to bicycle parking and end-of-trip facilities.

Controls

  • All new development must provide on-site bicycle parking in addition to other parking requirements, in accordance with the minimums specified in Table 3
  • Bicycle parking facilities must be designed and constructed in accordance with AS2890.3
  • Bicycle parking must address the following user categories:
  • Secure, covered all-day parking for employees and students
  • Co-living or hostel developments with low car parking provision
  • Permanent bicycle storage for residents
  • Short term visitor parking for shopping centres, commercial offices, industrial and other public and private buildings
  • All day parking at transport interchanges.
  • Bicycle parking for residents and staff must be located close to building entry/exits and lifts and prioritised over other parking types to ensure visibility, convenience and usage. Avoid locating bicycle parking in hidden niches, at the end of aisles and under staircases, etc
  • Where bicycle parking is in basement levels, it must be placed on the uppermost basement level close to exits and/ ramps and as near to ground level as possible
  • Bicycle paring areas must be clearly marked, easily accessible and avoid reliance on lifts for access. Ramp access is preferred for bicycle parking located at basement level/s
  • Bicycle parking spaces must be well-lit, allow for secure locking of both frame and wheels and be subject to passive surveillance.
  • Bicycle parking must be secure, weather protected, and constructed of durable, tamper resistant materials.
  • Bicycle parking must be designed to accommodate a variety of bicycle types, including cargo bikes, e-bikes, and other micromobility devices.
  • One-wheel racks are not acceptable nor are facilities that require a wheel to be removed
  • A safe and direct path of travel must be provided from bicycle parking areas to building entry/exit points. Paths must be marked and have a minimum width of 1.5m wide, include adequate turning space and maintain clear sight lines for safety
  • Visitor bicycle parking must be provided in an accessible on-grade location near major public entrances, away from pedestrian desire lines and clearly sign posted
  • Locker and end-of-trip facilities must be provided in accordance with the NSW Bicycle Guidelines to ensure good bicycle parking arrangements
  • End of trip facilities, where required, must be proportionate to the scale and nature of the development and incorporate secure lockers, showers and change rooms
  • End of trip facilities, where required, must be integrated into the building layout, not treated as leftover or residual space and be clearly signposted for easy access
  • Bicycle parking and end-of-trip facilities are to be provided in accordance with the rates in Tables 3 and 5, and part 3.3, Control b)
  • Where swimming pools and similar amenities are proposed in residential developments, bicycle parking should be co-located to allow shared use of facilities (such as showers and changing rooms) as end-of-trip facilities
  • A minimum of 25% of bicycle parking spaces must be capable of E-bike charging with appropriate power outlets provided. Elevated rack storage is not acceptable for E-Bike charging spaces.

Note

While there are no requirements stated for a dwelling house or semi-detached dwellings, the inclusion of a suitable internal/covered bike space is encouraged.

2.3. Car share

Explanation

Car share schemes provide an economical alternative to car ownership for residents and businesses. Several commercial schemes operate in Sydney providing on-line booking of vehicles linked to dedicated parking spots. These schemes are more viable in locations where private car ownership is discouraged or where available on street parking is limited. Membership of a car share scheme provides access to a network of new cars parked locally - without the expense of owning a car. Car sharing also helps to reduce the number of cars on the road and alleviate problems associated with traffic congestion. Council has also resolved to establish preferential parking for car-share and hybrid vehicles.

For large development, there may be an opportunity to provide dedicated on-site parking spaces for car share vehicles. This would be particularly effective for development on sites such as the University of NSW and Randwick Hospitals Campus, key strategic sites and within or adjoining commercial centres.

Car share schemes are effective on sites, or in areas of higher density with ready access to good public transport and services. To operate successfully car share vehicles need to be highly visible, easily and safely accessed at any time (whether on, or off the street) by residents and business operators on the site, as well as those in the surrounding precinct.

Car share spaces can also be dedicated for the exclusive use of building occupiers, if desired. In this case, the cost of the car share can be met through strata levies and must be organised by the developer.

Where car parking rates are being considered, Council will look more favourably on proposed reductions within close walking distance to areas of high public transport provision, including strategic bus corridors, and the light rail network and/or where a carshare scheme is provided on site.

Note

Any development can consider car share, however it is larger developments where a car share space/s are most encouraged by Council.

Objectives

The objectives for car share are to:

  • Encourage sustainable transport options and reduce private vehicle dependency by incentivising the provision of car share spaces in areas of high public transport accessibility
  • Increase car share usage as a means of reducing reliance on private vehicle ownership
  • Promote social inclusion by providing access to vehicles for households without private cars.

Controls

  • Car share spaces must be provided in residential, mixed use, shop top housing, co-living and/or commercial development, where public transport accessibility is high and/or where a Transport Assessment Study is required
  • Co-living developments, may be eligible for a parking credit equivalent to five standard parking spaces for each carshare space provided
  • The maximum number of carshare spaces within a co-living development shall generally not exceed one carshare space for every 50 rooms
  • For other residential or mixed-use developments, carshare credits will be considered by Council on a case-by-case basis, subject to demonstrated transport benefits
  • Car share spaces must be in convenient, accessible and secure areas with good visibility
  • Where located in a basement, carshare spaces are to be positioned near entry/exit points to enable easy access for non-residents of the building
  • Carshare spaces provided by a commercial operator must offer 24-hour public access, unless otherwise approved by Council
  • Car share spaces must be clearly marked with appropriate signage and pavement markings, in accordance with Transport for NSW (TfNSW) standards, indicating exclusive use by car share vehicles
  • Carshare schemes must be operational upon completion or occupation of the development to ensure immediate availability and uptake
  • Carshare spaces located on private property must be retained as common property under the management of the Owners Corporation of the site
  • Carshare spaces must not be converted to general parking spaces without prior approval from Council
  • A legal agreement or evidence of partnership with a recognised car share provider must be submitted with the DA.

2.4. Electric vehicles

Explanation

The integration of electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure in developments plays a vital role in supporting the transition to cleaner sustainable transport. In line with the National Construction Code (NCC), all parking spaces in Class 2, 3, 5, 6, 7b, 8, and 9 buildings, including residential apartments, commercial buildings, and retail premises, must be equipped with dedicated electrical distribution boards for EV charging.

As demand for EV continues to grow Council is committed to expanding this infrastructure across suitable locations. In addition to public facilities, it is essential that private properties are equipped to support EV charging. Consequently, all new major developments, as well as significant alterations or additions to existing major developments, will be required to provide the capacity for EV charging.

Objectives

The objectives for EVs are to:

  • Provide EV infrastructure to facilitate residents, occupants, contracted car share companies and visitors of buildings to charge their electric vehicles
  • Provide the infrastructure required to facilitate increased usage of electric vehicle charging equipment in allocated parking spaces.

Controls

  • Where a development has non-private parking spaces, EV charging equipment is to be installed at the following rates.
  • The lesser of:
  • 10% of the total number of all parking spaces in the development, or
  • the total number of non-private parking spaces.

Numbers are rounded up, if 0.5 or more, to the nearest whole number.

Note

Control (a) is a method of determining the number of non-private parking spaces for which EV charging equipment is to be installed. This provision does not relate to private parking space.

  • Each parking space for which EV charging equipment is required, is to be supplied with EV charging equipment with a minimum rated power output of 7kW (32A single phase)
  • EV charging equipment installed may include a combination of EV chargers of different power levels, at the discretion of the developer, subject to the minimum power level noted above
  • EV charging equipment is to be compliant with Australian Standards, marked with Regulatory Compliance Mark (RCM) markings, and equipped with OCPP 1.6J (or higher) communications capability
  • In accordance with the EV Distribution Board requirements of the NCC, the wiring enclosure system is to be identified to allow each car space to install an EV charger point. This system must allow for future installation of cabling to EV charger points and allow internet access using one of the following:
  • Cable tray of a size designed and calculated to be sufficient, is to be installed from the EV Distribution Board to within 5m of all parking bays allocated for in the EV Distribution Board, on that storey
  • An alternative to a cable tray may be provided, if it demonstrates the same or better than the requirements of provisions e (i) above.
  • EV charging equipment must include a billing mechanism that enables cost recovery for residents and visitors using the EV charging equipment. Development applications must clearly define how sub-metering or cost allocation will be managed by the incoming o wner's corporation when they take over operation of the site. Service agreements must not include vendor lockin clauses and a clear pathway must be provided for the owner's corporation to make alternative billing arrangements without a punitive exit clauses from a service provider.
  • Development must demonstrate the capability of tracking interval data of the building electrical consumer mains. This may be achieved through the installation of a smart meter or equivalent technology.

Residential developments must install a minimum of two 'Level 2' AC fast EV charging points within common parking areas. The circuit is to be suitably located to provide convenient, shared access for residents (and where relevant, commercial users). The charging infrastructure must:

  • Be equipped with 62196-2 Type 2 socket
  • Provide up to 22kW or 32A three phase charging port
  • Be installed on a dedicated circuit
  • Support monitoring and individual billing via OCPP-compatible software
  • Include a dedicated parking space for EVs to park and charge safely and conveniently.
  • Commercial developments must provide EV charging infrastructure in accordance with the National Construction Code (NCC). A minimum of 10% of all car parking spaces in public parking areas must be equipped with 'Level 2' AC fast charging EV charging points. The circuit is to be suitably located to provide for convenient, shared access for commercial users. The charging point must:
  • Be equipped with 62196-2 Type 2 socket
  • Provide up to 22kW or 32A three phase charging per port
  • Be installed on a dedicated circuit
  • Support monitoring and individual billing via OCPP-compatible software
  • Include dedicated EV parking spaces for safe and convenient access to park and charge.
  • All EV charging infrastructure must be installed by appropriately licenced professionals and comply with relevant standards and regulations including Section J9D4 'Facilities for electric vehicle charging equipment' in NCC 2022 Volume One - Building Code of Australia, which outlines requirements for provision and design of distribution boards to support electric vehicle charging in car parks
  • A statement prepared by a suitably qualified person must be submitted with the DA confirming that the proposal will be able to meet the electric vehicle requirements of this DCP and the applicable provisions of the NCC.

2.5. Resident parking schemes

Explanation

Resident parking permits are intended to exempt eligible residents from certain kerbside time restrictions in areas where on-street parking demand is high due to shoppers, commuters and visitors. These circumstances typically occur in and around business or neighbourhood shopping centres, and major activity generators such as the Randwick Education and Health Specialised Centre, public swimming pools, sports fields and beaches.

To support sustainable transport outcomes and reduce reliance on private vehicles, resident parking permits will not be issued to occupants of new residential developments that include onsite parking approved under this DCP. This restriction will be imposed as a condition of development consent, recorded on Section 10.7 Planning Certificates, and must be disclosed to all prospective purchasers and tenants.

Objectives

  • Improve the amenity for residents who do not have access to off-street parking and who live in areas with time-limited on-street parking, in accordance with the NSW Resident Parking Scheme.
  • Encourage sustainable transport and reduce car dependency.

Controls

  • No resident parking permits will be issued for new residential development, co-living, boarding houses or for significant alterations and additions to mixed use, shop top housing, or residential flat buildings, that result in a net increase in dwellings. This restriction must be communicated to all prospective owners and tenants.
  • A notice must be displayed in the foyer or common area of all affected buildings advising occupants that the building is not eligible for on-street resident parking permit exemptions.

3. Development Application (DA) requirements

3.1. Traffic and parking study requirements

Explanation

To effectively manage transport demand generated by new development, applicants must provide appropriate assessments that demonstrate how transport impacts will be addressed. These assessments help Council ensure that development does not unreasonably increase congestion or parking demand, and that sustainable transport options are considered and encouraged.

Objectives

  • Ensure development proposals are supported by appropriate and proportionate transport and traffic studies.
  • Minimise congestion and parking pressures generated by new development.
  • Promote sustainable transport choices, including public transport, walking and cycling.

Controls

  • Depending on the nature and scale of the development, one or more supporting studies may be required to be submitted with the development application:

Transport Impact Assessment (TIA)

  • Green Travel Plan (GTP)
  • Parking and Access Study
  • Delivery and Servicing Plan

Construction Traffic Management Plan (CTMP)

Note

Table 1: Vehicle parking rates , sets out where one or more of these studies is required, depending on the proposed type/s of development.

  • The TIA must be prepared by a qualified traffic engineer. The study/report must be signed by the author and include their professional qualifications and membership number with the Institute of Engineers, Australia. This is to ensure that new developments do not unreasonably increase congestion and parking demands in busy areas, and to encourage developers to adopt sustainable transport options and new residents to use public transport, car share, walking and cycling.

3.2. Transport Impact Assessment (TIA)

Explanation

A TIA is a technical investigation into the transport and safety issues that might arise from a development. This includes impacts to pedestrians, cyclists, motorists and passengers, public transport users, and freight and servicing vehicles. It also assesses the transport related impacts on the surrounding transportation network that are generated by a development and how those impacts are to be managed. Such a study recognises the role of traffic within a broader transport system that includes public transport, walking and cycling.

Objectives

  • Ensure comprehensive assessment of transport impacts for new development.
  • Support integration of development with existing and planned transport infrastructure.
  • Maintain safe, efficient and accessible movement for all users.
  • Minimise adverse impacts on the road network, parking supply and surrounding amenity.

Controls

The TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment should be used to inform the scope and detail of the TIA, which complements the matters listed in this DCP. A TIA assessment must include the following:

  • The accessibility of the site by various transport modes including car, public transport, walking and cycling
  • Capacity of the public transport network to service the site during peak, off peak and weekend periods
  • Mode share targets and strategies to reduce car dependency
  • Measures to minimise car travel and maximise other modes including public transport use, cycling or walking
  • Compliance with the requirements of the LEP and DCP
  • Justification of car parking provision and site servicing arrangements in accordance with the objectives of the Randwick LEP and DCP
  • Proposed allocation of parking spaces by dwelling types for residential developments
  • Access provisions for people with mobility impairments
  • Trip generation estimates and impacts of trips on the road transport network
  • Integration of trips generated with existing infrastructure and identification of necessary improvements or upgrades to public transport services and infrastructure (e.g. bus shelters), pedestrian systems, bicycle routes, and the road network
  • Mitigation strategies for any adverse impacts of the development on movement systems
  • Means of improving access to the site having regard to vehicular, pedestrian, cycle and public transport access
  • Impacts on and means of improving pedestrian accessibility to public transport (including proximity to services), shops, schools, open spaces, community centres and the like
  • Pedestrian safety, including appropriate locations of access driveways
  • Availability of on street parking and potential controls to discourage long term residential parking demand generated by the development.
  • Trip generation must be assessed using the TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment which provides standard vehicular trip generating rates for both daily and peak hour vehicle trips. Comparative surveys of similar developments to the proposal, can also be used. The vehicle trip generation assessment must consider:
  • The peak activity periods of the proposed development
  • The peak activity on the adjacent road network
  • Whether road upgrades, traffic management or pedestrian safety measures are required to accommodate the increased movement on the system.
  • The TIA must include a comparison of vehicle trip generation rates contained in the ' TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment' , parking availability, access to public transport and proximity to neighbourhood shopping centres, community facilities and open spaces. Adjustments factors for each land use may include:
  • Mode split by time period
  • Persons per vehicle
  • Trip purpose
  • Availability of on-site parking.
  • Where necessary, traffic mitigation measures can be incorporated to ameliorate the impact of traffic and parking generated by the development including traffic signals, signs, pedestrian crossings, channelisation, roundabouts, angled parking, and traffic calming devices, storage days and median islands.

3.3. Green Travel Plan

Explanation

A Green Travel Plan (GTP) is a workplace plan developed to make it easier for employees to get to and from work and reduce reliance on private vehicles and parking spaces. Such a plan typically includes support for walking, cycling, car-pooling and public transport use. It is an important part of managing the transport demand generated by a development.

Objectives

The objectives of a Green Travel Plan are to

  • Ensure developments are supported by effective, site-specific transport planning.
  • Provide appropriate end-of-trip facilities to encourage walking and cycling.
  • Improve accessibility and awareness of sustainable transport options for occupants.
  • Establish clear implementation, monitoring and review mechanisms to support long-term travel behaviour change.

Controls

  • A GTP is to be based on the findings of the TIA
  • The GTP must:
  • Be prepared by a suitably qualified transport or traffic consultant, in consultation with Transport for NSW where necessary
  • Include clear objectives and mode share targets aimed at reducing private car use and increasing public and active transport. Targets must be measurable, achievable, and linked to defined implementation timeframes.
  • I dentify specific tools, actions and measures to achieve the stated objectives and mode share targets, including any carparking management strategies required to support sustainable transport outcomes.
  • Outline implementation responsibilities, including roles and responsibilities of relevant staff and procedures for ongoing management of the Plan
  • A monitoring and review program to assess travel behaviour and the effectiveness of the Plan.
  • End of trip facilities must be provided proportionate to the scale and nature of the development
  • End of trip facilities must be provided in developments in accordance with Tables 3 and 5 at the rates specified. Refer also to the Transport for NSW, Walking and Cycling Program Guidelines (2018-19) and the NSW Bike Plan (May 2010) Active Transport Strategy (TfNSW) and Council's Active Transport Plan - Walking and Cycling.
  • The GTP should include a Travel Access Guide (TAG) incorporating the following information:
  • A comprehensive map showing all modes of public and active transport, including buses (private and public), trains, walking and cycling routes, as well as times for these public transport options.
  • Information advising that service routes, timetables for buses, trains, light rail and ferries and walking routes are available on the Transport for NSW website
  • Number and location of End of Trip facilities and bicycle parking (eg bicycle racks, showers, lockers, change rooms)
  • Location of any carpooling/share car spaces where available.

Note

Refer to the TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment 2024.

3.4. Parking And Access Report (PAAR)

Explanation

A PAAR may be required, should the development result in a parking shortfall.

Objective

1. Ensure adequate assessment of on-street parking availability to minimise parking impacts from development

Control

  • The PAAR should incorporate a survey of available on-street parking within 100m walking distance from the site demonstrating sufficient availability to mitigate any impacts. Surveys should reflect typical conditions and must not be undertaken during school holidays

3.5. Construction Traffic Management Plan (CTMP)

Explanation

A CTMP is a practical response to ensuring that demolition and construction works do not adversely impact on the public domain - on pedestrian, cyclist and vehicular movements, and on-street parking in an area.

Objective

1. Ensure construction and site activities are managed to minimise disruption to traffic, public transport operations, and pedestrian movement.

Control

  • A CMTP is to detail how proposed development located on busy roads, bus or light rail stops or on difficult sites will be able to undertake loading and unloading, demolition and construction including the manoeuvring of trucks in and out of a site with minimum disruption to vehicular and pedestrian traffic or transportation networks.

3.6. Traffic generating development

Explanation

Under the State Environmental Planning Policy (Transport and Infrastructure) 2021, Council is required to refer certain types of DAs to Transport for New South Wales (TfNSW).

Objective

1. Ensure traffic-generating development is appropriately assessed and coordinated with relevant authorities to minimise impacts on the transport network and surrounding community

Controls

  • The specific development types subject to referral are outlined in the SEPP
  • Any temporary signage or line marking required on Council-managed roads must be clearly justified and may be subject to community consultation and referral to the Local Transport Forum.

4. Vehicle, motorcycle and scooter requirements

4.1. Relationship to other standards and policy

DAs requiring car parking will need to consider the following documents:

  • Australian Standards (AS)
  • AS 1428 Design for access and mobility
  • AS 2890 Parking Facilities series:
  • AS 2890.1 Off-street car parking
  • AS 2890.2 Off-street commercial vehicle facilities
  • AS 2890.5 On-street parking
  • AS 2890.6 Off-street parking for people with a disability
  • State Environmental Planning Policy (Transport and Infrastructure) 2021
  • TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment 2024 (GTIA)
  • Austroads guides

4.2. Vehicle parking rates

Explanation

Vehicle parking rates apply to all forms of development, including new development, alterations and additions to existing development and changes of use. The Provision of motorcycle and scooter parking is encouraged recognising these modes as efficient and lower-emission transport alternatives.

Service delivery vehicle parking rates are provided in Table 6 of this Part of the DCP. Bicycle parking requirements are set out in Tables 3, 4 and 5.

Objectives

  • Ensure an appropriate and efficient provision of off-street vehicle parking that supports the operational needs and accessibility of development.
  • Minimise reliance on private vehicle use by aligning parking provision with access to public transport, centres and active transport networks.
  • Encourage a shift towards more sustainable transport modes, including walking, cycling and public transport, by avoiding the over - provision of car parking.
  • Support the creation of high-quality, people-focused urban environments by balancing parking provision with urban design, public domain and land use outcomes.
  • Facilitate flexible and context-responsive parking outcomes that reflect the nature, scale and location of development, including proximity to public transport and local services.

Controls

  • Development must comply with the vehicle parking rates as detailed in Table 1: Vehicle parking rates. Any parking in excess of the prescribed parking rates will be included in the calculation of Gross Floor Area (GFA).
  • Parking must be provided for service and delivery vehicles, bicycles and persons with a disability in accordance with the relevant provisions of this DCP having regard to the nature and scale of the development.
  • Where a parking rate is not specified in Table 1, parking provision for the proposed development must be determined having regard to the Transport for NSW Transport

Impact Assessment Guidelines. Alternatively, a Transport Assessment Study may be submitted for consideration to justify an appropriate parking provision.

  • For mixed use development the allocation and distribution of car spaces between different uses must be clearly identified on the DA plans.

4.3. Accessible parking requirements

Explanation

The Federal Government's Disability Discrimination Act 1992 ( DDA ) sets the legal framework to ensure equal access for people with a disability. The National Construction Code (NCC) and Disability (Access to Premises - Buildings) Standards establish the minimum requirements for accessible car parking.

Objective

  • All development is to provide accessible car parking spaces for people with a disability as set out in the NCC and the relevant (and most current) Australian Standard.

Control

  • The dimensions for car spaces, including headroom and access requirements for people with a disability, are set out in AS 2890.6 2022 .

4.4. Parking for adaptable housing

Explanation

Where adaptable housing units are provided in accordance with part C3 Universal, adaptable and accessible housing of this DCP, the car parking rate will be equivalent to that required for residential flat buildings.

Objectives

The objectives for parking for adaptable housing are to:

  • Ensure that the design of parking areas is safe and accessible with best practice standards for people with a disability

Provide enough designated car parking spaces for vehicles used by people with a disability.

Controls

  • Parking must comply with the minimum requirements of AS 4299 Adaptable Housing regarding car parking or alternatively with the access and dimensional standards for car spaces for people with a disability as specified in the NCC and the Australian Standard AS 2890.6
  • Accessible parking spaces for people with a disability must be located close to building entrances, lifts or access points and connected by a continuous accessible path of travel
  • The location of accessible parking spaces must be clearly signposted at the entrance to the car park
  • Accessible parking spaces must be well lit and clearly line marked
  • Signage and directional information within parking areas must be legible, well-lit, and designed for ease of use and safety
  • Where lifts are used to access parking areas, they must include audio cues and tactile control panels to support universal access
  • Accessible car parking spaces allocated to adaptable units must form part of the strata lot within the strata scheme and must not to be designated as utility lots or common property

4.5. Car park location and design

Explanation

The Australian Standards and TfNSW guidelines provide the base requirements for parking location and design. Car park location and design need to be carefully considered to ensure pedestrian safety, clear sight lines and to maintain streetscape character and amenity.

In older established areas, with uniform streetscapes and heritage conservation areas, the provision of car parking needs to maintain the character of the area and the significance of the item or conservation area.

Objectives

  • Ensure car parking is located and designed to support safe, functional, and efficient vehicle, pedestrian, and cyclist movement.
  • Minimise impacts on on-street parking, pedestrian amenity, and streetscape continuity
  • Maintain and enhance streetscape character, particularly in established and heritage areas.
  • Reduce the visual prominence of parking, vehicle access and loading areas within the public domain

Controls

  • Minimise loss of existing on-street parking supply by:
  • Careful location of crossings and laybacks
  • Tapering the driveway at the property boundary
  • Amalgamating driveway crossings with adjoining property where possible
  • Considering the overall streetscape, continuity of footpaths and the need for safe pedestrian movement.
  • Ensure pedestrian and cycling safety is maintained or improved
  • Where feasible, vehicle access and/or loading are to be provided from secondary streets or rear lanes and set back a minimum of 6m from intersections to improve safety and reduce visual impact
  • Basement carpark access must comply with the requirements of B8 Water managemen t
  • Vehicle access points and loading areas are to be designed as visually recessive elements within the building elevation to minimise their prominence
  • Parking is to be accommodated underground wherever possible to preserve streetscape character and reduce surface-level congestion
  • Sub-basement car parking structures must not exceed 1.2m above existing ground level

Refer to other relevant parts of this DCP, for example sections that address residential or heritage considerations for detail on car parking design, provision and location particularly for older areas or areas with heritage value.

Note

In some cases, it may not be possible to provide off-street car spaces.

4.6. Parking layout, configuration and dimensions

Explanation

The specific requirements for parking layout and dimensions (for car spaces, aisles, disabled, grades, etc.) are provided in the relevant Australian Standard and the TfNSW guidelines. All development must comply with these standards as a minimum level of provision to ensure car parking facilities are efficient, adequate and safe.

In residential areas, smaller car spaces are sometimes sought for dwelling houses or semidetached dwellings on narrow lots with access from the primary street frontage. These carports or hard stand spaces may only be suitable where they are able to accommodate medium sized cars as this avoids overhanging the footpath and creating a potential sight and physical hazard to pedestrians and other road users. Off street parking often also involves the loss of valuable on-streetcar parking spaces and disrupts the continuity and safety of footpaths.

Objectives

  • Provide parking spaces and access arrangements that accommodate a range of users and vehicle types
  • Minimise impacts on pedestrian safety, footpath continuity and on-street parking

Controls

  • The design and minimum dimensions of off-street car parking spaces must be in accordance with the requirements of AS 2890.1 Parking Facilities
  • A reduction in car space length to a maximum of 5m may be considered where site constraints - such as limited lot width or reduced front setbacks - are characteristic of small lots, semi-detached, or attached dwellings. In such scenarios the applicant must:
  • Demonstrate site specific design constraints
  • Maintain safe vehicle access and egress
  • Comply with relevant standards for small car spaces
  • Provide a swept path analysis where applicable.
  • Motorcycle parking spaces must be a minimum 2.5m by 1.2m and clearly marked
  • Motorcycle spaces are to be designed and located so they are not vulnerable to being struck by manoeuvring vehicles
  • Motorcycle spaces must be located on flat and even surfaces as they rely on sidestands to park
  • In all development except dwelling houses, semi-detached dwellings or attached dwellings, all vehicles must enter and exit in a forward direction.
  • For development located on a main or arterial road, all vehicles must enter and exit in a forward direction
  • Unless otherwise stated, development is to comply with the relevant Australian Standard and the TfNSW guidelines for car parking layout, dimensions, aisle widths, grades, access requirements for different uses and users (e.g. those with disabilities), driveway widths, service and delivery needs.
  • Tandem parking spaces are generally discouraged unless where it can be demonstrated that:
  • the operation of the tandem parking arrangement will not adversely impact the adjacent road or footpath area
  • the proposal is located within a low traffic area
  • all vehicle movements associated with the tandem arrangement will occur wholly within the site and would not require vehicles to queue, wait, or undertake manoeuvres within the public road or footway.
  • The parking layout will be designed to ensure safe, efficient and practical operation for all users, including consideration of peak period vehicle movements and the management of potential conflicts between vehicles parked in tandem

Refer also to the relevant parts of this DCP for car parking details relating to specific land uses such as residential, commercial, industrial and specific locations such as UNSW.

4.7. Access to dwellings elevated above retaining walls

Explanation

The historical subdivisions in the coastal areas of Randwick City have created several urban blocks that are elevated above public roads due to the sloping topography. The frontage to these allotments is supported by masonry block (often sandstone) retaining walls aligned with the carriageway boundaries, and with public footpaths running above.

The provision of off-street parking to these sites often proves to be problematic as it necessitates significant demolition and modification to the retaining walls. In some circumstances, the height of the retaining wall does not provide sufficient clearance for parking facilities as required by the Australian Standard.

The public footpaths above may need to be raised along the frontage of the development site, which further compromises the visual integrity of the retaining walls, streetscape character and pedestrian accessibility. Any successive developments for vehicular access would incrementally remove wall sections and lead to cumulative visual impacts.

Due to the likely adverse implications on streetscape amenity, the partial demolition of existing retaining walls within the public domain for the sole purpose of gaining vehicular access to a private property will generally not be supported.

Objectives

  • Protect the integrity, character and continuity of existing retaining walls, particularly those of heritage or streetscape significance
  • Maintain the visual amenity and consistency of streetscapes in areas with elevated lots and established topography
  • Ensure safe and accessible pedestrian environments, including preserving existing footpath levels and usability

Controls

  • Any provision of vehicular access to dwellings must minimise demolition, modification and damage to existing retaining walls within the public domain
  • Double width driveway and entry to on-site parking involving full or part removal of retaining walls in the public domain is not permitted
  • Development must not involve any significant change to the existing gradients of public footpaths above the retaining walls, except to facilitate equitable access
  • The creation of an access driveway must not jeopardise the safety of pedestrians and vehicles
  • Pedestrian and cyclist entry points must be separated from vehicle accessing driveways, to ensure safety of vulnerable road users and to avoid vehicle conflict
  • Driveway access and front yards should be separated by physical barriers (e.g. wall, fence, etc)
  • Sight distances at driveways are to be compliant with AS 2890.1 and AS2890.2
  • Works that require alteration or replacement of landscape elements and structures (such as handrails) adjacent to the public footpaths situated above retaining walls must be compatible with the streetscape character.

4.8. Mechanical Parking Devices

Explanation

Mechanical parking devices, such as vehicle turntables and automated parking platforms, may be considered on constrained sites where conventional on-site manoeuvring cannot be achieved. While these systems can improve access efficiency and reduce the need for extensive driveway areas, they also introduce operational, safety, and public domain considerations that require careful assessment.

The operation of mechanical parking systems has the potential to influence pedestrian and vehicle movements on the adjoining road and footpath, particularly in situations where cycle times, queuing, or system malfunctions may cause vehicles to pause or encroach into the public domain.

In addition, noise and vibration generated by mechanical components may affect neighbouring properties if not appropriately mitigated.

Objectives

  • Ensure mechanical parking devices are only used where necessary and operate safely, efficiently and reliably.
  • Minimise impacts on the public domain, including pedestrian and vehicle movements, and prevent queuing or encroachment onto roads and footpaths.
  • Protect the amenity of adjoining properties by minimising noise, vibration and visual impacts.

Controls

  • The use of mechanical parking systems e.g. car lifts, car stackers and turntables, should be minimised especially where queuing or safety concerns may arise.
  • Mechanical parking devices may only be permitted where it is clearly demonstrated that their installation and operation will not adversely impact the public domain, adjoining properties, or traffic and pedestrian movements.
  • All mechanical parking devices must be located wholly within the site.
  • Development applications proposing mechanical parking devices must include an assessment prepared by a suitably qualified traffic engineer addressing:
  • the operational characteristics of the device, including cycle times and capacity
  • Technical specifications of the proposed system (the onus is on the applicant to demonstrate the mechanical device can be accommodated within the design space available)
  • potential for vehicle queuing and any risk of encroachment onto the road or footpath
  • pedestrian and vehicle safety impacts
  • noise and vibration impacts
  • sightline and visibility considerations for vehicles entering or exiting the site.
  • Swept paths based on the B99 design template in AS 2890.1 demonstrating satisfactory ingress and egress can be achieved into the mechanical device
  • All manoeuvring associated with the mechanical parking device must occur within the site and must not rely on the public road or footpath.
  • The device must be designed and installed to ensure safe, reliable and efficient operation at all times, including during peak demand periods.
  • A maintenance and operational management plan must be submitted with the application which outlines servicing requirements, procedures for breakdowns, and measures to ensure the device does not obstruct the public domain in the event of malfunction.
  • Where car lifts are proposed to enter basement carparking;
  • A passing bay will be required in front of the car lift unless it can be satisfactorily demonstrated by way of a queueing analysis that the probability of vehicle conflict is minimal.
  • Car lifts are to be in accordance with AS 1735.1
  • Car lifts accessing further mechanical devices such as stackers or turntables will generally not be supported.

5. Parking rates - vehicles, motorcycles and scooters (excluding K2K, RJTC, WLHA)

This section of the DCP provides the applicable car parking rates for vehicles, motorcycles and scooters for new development and significant alterations in the whole Randwick LGA, except for the Kensington and Kingsford Town Centres (K2K), the Randwick Junction Town Centre (RJTC) and the five Well Located Housing Areas (WLHA) (formally known as HIAs).

Where development comprises an extension, modification or change of use to an existing development, Council will generally only require that additional parking be provided to cater for the additional demands arising from increases in floor space or changes in use.

Note

Parking calculations should be rounded to the nearest whole number. Where the fraction is 0.5, then the figure must be rounded up to the next whole number.

8. Exceptions to parking rates

Explanation

The DCP sets appropriate parking rates for most development types and conditions, however it is also recognised that variations may be appropriate where developments incorporate suitable and sustainable transport alternatives.

In some cases, it may not be physically feasible, or aesthetically appropriate, to provide on-site parking - for example where off street parking would impact the frontage of a heritage item or compromise areas of significant streetscape value.

It is the responsibility of the applicant through the development assessment processes, to demonstrate that parking provision is adequate, or that the overall planning benefits of the proposed outweigh any shortfall in parking.

Objectives:

  • Ensure any variation to parking rates does not result in unacceptable impacts on local traffic, on-street parking, or safety.
  • Support developments that incorporate sustainable and integrated transport options, reducing reliance on private vehicles.
  • Require a robust, evidence-based justification demonstrating that any shortfall in parking is appropriate and will not adversely impact the surrounding area.

Controls

  • Any proposed variation to the prescribed parking rates must address the following considerations relevant to the development:
  • The type and scale of the development and its potential impact on local traffic and parking conditions
  • Comparative analysis of parking provision in similar recent developments
  • Existing on-street parking provision available prior to the proposed development
  • Site specific building constraints that limit parking provision
  • Heritage and urban design considerations including significant streetscape elements such as sandstone retaining walls, significant mature trees and any other valued features
  • Availability of on street and public parking in the vicinity, and proximity to public transport services
  • Accessibility to local services, employment hubs, retail centres and recreational facilities
  • Safety considerations for vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists
  • Provision of integrated and sustainable transport options within the development such as bicycle parking, car share and EV Charging.

9. Service and delivery vehicles

9.1. Service and delivery vehicle requirements and rates

Explanation

The number of service bays required for a development depends on the size and servicing requirements of the type of development. The following rates are based on the TfNSW Guideline. Major developments should quantify their service vehicle requirements through new surveys of similar developments.

Development Applications must demonstrate that servicing, loading and waste management arrangements are designed in accordance with the principles and requirements of TfNSW including The Last Mile Toolkit and relevant TfNSW policies. This includes the provision of adequate on-site servicing capacity, accommodating the anticipated freight and waste task, ensuring safe and efficient vehicle access and manoeuvring and minimising adverse impacts on the surrounding road network, kerbside operations and public domain amenity.

Note

Development applications must include plans that clearly show how vehicles will enter, exit, and move within the site safely and smoothly, while minimising impacts on nearby roads, kerbside use, and public spaces

Objectives

  • Ensure developments provide adequate on-site servicing, loading and delivery facilities that meet the operational needs of the development.
  • Minimise impacts of servicing and delivery activities on the surrounding road network, kerbside operations, pedestrian amenity and the public domain.

Controls

  • Development must comply with the minimum requirements for the parking of service and delivery vehicles as set in Table 6: Service and delivery vehicle rates.
  • Service vehicle dimensions, layout and service/loading bays must comply with Australian Standard AS 2890.1 (off street parking) and AS 2890.2 ( off street commercial vehicle facilities) as applicable.
  • Should on site waste collection by Council be required, loading bays must be designed to accommodate Council's waste collection vehicles, with the bin presentation area immediately adjacent. Technical specifications of Councils current waste vehicle fleet can be obtained from Council's Engineers
  • Driveways must be minimised along primary streets and along active frontages with no additional vehicle crossings permitted unless it can be demonstrated that there are no feasible alternative access arrangements.
  • All accessways, driveways, and servicing areas must accommodate the nominated vehicle in accordance with:
  • AS 2890.1 - Parking facilities (Off-streetcar parking)
  • AS 2890.2 - Off-street commercial vehicle facilities
  • AS 2890.6 - Off-street parking for people with disabilities
  • Driveways and crossovers must prioritise pedestrian safety and amenity.
  • Development applications must include swept path analysis (based on the appropriate service and delivery vehicle) prepared by a suitably qualified traffic engineer demonstrating satisfactory ingress and egress.
